3 marks: Describes a change to the investigation and gives a reason linked to the evidence
2 marks: Identifies a change to the investigation, with limited reason
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Link each change to a specific uncontrolled variable in the scenario, such as the soil source or the sprinkler.
Justify why each change makes the results valid, rather than listing changes that would be good practice anyway.
commonStudentErrors: Proposing a change, such as more samples, that does not address the uncontrolled variables.
Saying the trial should be abandoned, which does not modify the investigation.
Justifying changes without saying how they make the results valid.

sampleAnswers.answer: The class should modify the investigation so that the only difference between samples is the variable being tested. First, all samples should come from one paddock, or the soil type should be recorded and matched, because soil from different paddocks differs in texture and organic matter, which would make any comparison invalid. Second, the sprinkler should be replaced with a fixed-rate method, such as pouring a standard volume at a set speed, so each sample receives the same input. Third, the class should check each sample's starting moisture and dry weight before the trial, and repeat the trial with more samples. These changes are justified because they remove the uncontrolled variables revealed by the new evidence. This makes the results valid evidence about infiltration, rather than about the soil source or the watering method.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by justifying each change with sustained reasoning about the uncontrolled variables and the validity of the results.

sampleAnswers.answer: The class should fix the sprinkler to a constant rate, because its uneven rate is an uncontrolled variable that the new evidence has revealed.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by justifying one change to the method with a sound link to the new evidence. It does not justify further changes or explain how the results become valid, so it does not reach the 5-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The class should use soil from one paddock only.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying one change with limited reason. It does not say how the change makes the results valid, so it does not reach the 3-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Explain why current scientific knowledge is both contestable and testable by further inquiry

prompts.question: DESCRIBE one further investigation that could test whether the continents have moved apart over time.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A Year 11 class is studying the history of plate tectonics. In 1912 Alfred Wegener proposed that the continents had once been joined and had since drifted apart. Most geologists rejected his idea at the time, largely because he could not explain what moved the continents.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes one specific investigation and what its results would show about the continents moving apart
2 marks: Identifies an investigation that could test the claim, with limited detail of how it works
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Name one specific investigation, such as repeated measurement of the positions of the continents, and say what result would support the idea.
A useful test must be able to show the idea is wrong as well as right. Naming a test without a method stays in the lower rows.
commonStudentErrors: Retelling the history of Wegener's idea rather than describing an investigation that could test it.
Naming a test, such as looking at rocks, without saying what result would show the continents moving apart.

sampleAnswers.answer: Geologists could measure the present-day movement of the continents using GPS receivers fixed to sites on each landmass, repeated over several years. If the distances between continents steadily increase, the investigation supports the idea. The claim is contestable until it is tested, which shows that scientific knowledge is testable through further inquiry.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing one specific investigation, repeated GPS measurement of the continents, and what its results would show about them moving apart.

sampleAnswers.answer: Geologists could use satellites to check whether the continents are moving apart.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying an investigation that could test the idea, with limited detail of how the measurement works.

sampleAnswers.answer: Geologists could look at rocks on different continents.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by providing some relevant information. It names no clear test of whether the continents have moved apart.

prompts.question: ANALYSE how the history of continental drift shows that scientific knowledge is both contestable and testable.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A Year 11 class is writing a short report on how scientific ideas change over time. Wegener's continental drift hypothesis of 1912 was rejected for decades because he could not explain what moved the continents. Seafloor magnetic patterns and seafloor spreading, studied from the 1960s, later supported the theory of plate tectonics.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Analyses with sustained and specific reference to continental drift how its history shows that knowledge is both contestable and testable
4 marks: Analyses the history of continental drift with relevant evidence, showing that knowledge is contestable or testable
3 marks: Explains how continental drift was contested or tested, with some relevant evidence
2 marks: Identifies a relevant example of continental drift, with limited explanation
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Use the history of continental drift as specific evidence: the 1912 proposal, the objection about what moved the continents and the later seafloor data.
Analyse both halves of the statement, showing why the idea was open to challenge and why it could be tested, rather than describing one side only.
A strong answer explains what the history reveals about the nature of scientific knowledge, not just what happened in order.
commonStudentErrors: Retelling the history of plate tectonics without linking events to contestable or testable knowledge.
Saying scientific knowledge changes, without using the continental drift example to show it.
Describing the seafloor evidence as proof that ended all debate, rather than as support that led to acceptance.

sampleAnswers.answer: Wegener's 1912 continental drift hypothesis was contestable because he could not explain what moved the continents, so most geologists rejected it for decades. It was also testable: matching coastlines and Mesosaurus fossils on separate continents were evidence that could be checked. Geologists at the time demanded a mechanism before accepting a new claim, so the idea stayed contested. Further inquiry in the 1960s, including magnetic patterns on the seafloor, supported seafloor spreading, which gave the hypothesis a mechanism. The history shows that scientific knowledge is contestable while key parts are missing, and testable as new evidence is gathered. Each step shows how a claim is challenged, tested and then revised as further evidence arrives, which is how scientific knowledge develops.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row by analysing how the continental drift history shows knowledge is both contestable, because the mechanism was missing, and testable, because the coastline and fossil evidence could be checked.

sampleAnswers.answer: Continental drift was rejected because Wegener could not explain what moved the continents. Later seafloor evidence supported the idea, which shows that scientific knowledge can change.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining how the idea was contested and later tested, with some relevant evidence. It does not analyse both halves of the statement.

sampleAnswers.answer: Scientists can change their minds when new evidence is found.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by providing some relevant information. It makes a general point about changing ideas without using the continental drift example.

dotPoints.description: Construct evidence-based arguments and recognise the role of peer review in the evaluation of scientific practices, solutions or conclusions

prompts.question: OUTLINE the role that peer review would play in checking the group's conclusion before the council accepts it.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A Year 11 group sampled a local creek for two months after a new wetland was built upstream. Their data show lower nitrate levels than before the wetland existed. They want to tell the local council that the wetland has improved the creek's water quality.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Outlines how independent scientists would check the methods, data and conclusions before the council relies on them
2 marks: Identifies that other scientists review the work, with limited detail of what they check
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Name the role precisely: independent experts test the methods, data and conclusions before the findings are relied on.
Link the role to this group's work, such as the two-month sampling period or other causes of lower nitrates, rather than peer review in general.
commonStudentErrors: Saying peer review proves the group's conclusion is correct.
Describing peer review as the council voting on the findings, rather than experts evaluating the methods and data.

sampleAnswers.answer: Peer review means independent scientists check the group's methods, data and scientific conclusions before the council relies on them. They would test whether two months of sampling is enough to show the effect of the wetland, and whether other causes, such as rainfall, could explain the lower nitrate readings. This makes the evidence-based arguments more reliable.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by outlining how independent scientists would check the methods, data and conclusions before the council relies on them, including alternative causes such as rainfall.

sampleAnswers.answer: Other scientists would review the work before the council uses it.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying that other scientists review the work. It does not say what they check.

sampleAnswers.answer: Scientists would look at the group's findings.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by providing some relevant information. It mentions scientists looking at the findings but gives no role in their evaluation.

prompts.question: CONSTRUCT an evidence-based argument, for the council, that supports the group's claim. Include one way that peer review could test it.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A Year 11 group sampled a local creek for two months after a new wetland was built upstream. Their data show lower nitrate levels than before the wetland existed. They want to tell the local council that the wetland has improved the creek's water quality.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Constructs a sustained evidence-based argument for the claim and explains how peer review would test it
4 marks: Constructs a clear evidence-based argument for the claim using the data, with a named check from peer review
3 marks: Constructs a basic argument using some of the data, with limited reference to peer review
2 marks: Identifies a relevant point from the data, with limited argument
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Build the argument from the group's own data, such as lower nitrate levels after the wetland was built, and link each point to a reason.
Show the limits of the evidence, such as one season of data or other causes of lower nitrates, because this is what makes the argument scientific.
Make the peer review point specific: independent scientists check the methods, data and alternative explanations before the council relies on the conclusion.
commonStudentErrors: Writing a persuasive opinion about the wetland with no reasoning drawn from the data.
Saying peer review would make the claim true, rather than testing whether the data support it.
Ignoring alternative causes, such as rainfall or farming, and presenting the wetland as the only explanation.

sampleAnswers.answer: The group can argue that the wetland has improved the creek's water quality, because their data show lower nitrate levels than before the wetland was built. This is consistent with wetlands removing nitrate from runoff, so the evidence-based arguments are scientifically plausible. A stronger argument would also compare readings from the same sites taken before the wetland existed, so the comparison is fair. However, two months of data from one season cannot prove the claim, and changes in rainfall or nearby farming could also lower nitrate levels. Peer review would test the claim by having independent scientists check the methods, the data and these alternative causes before the council accepts it.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row by constructing a sustained evidence-based argument for the claim, weighing the limits of two months of data and explaining how peer review would test it.

sampleAnswers.answer: The wetland may have improved the creek because the group's data show lower nitrate levels. Peer review would check whether the data support the claim.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by constructing a basic argument from some of the data, with reference to peer review. It does not weigh the limits of the evidence or alternative causes.

sampleAnswers.answer: Lower nitrate levels suggest the wetland is working.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by providing some relevant information. It states a conclusion from the data but gives no reasoning and does not mention peer review.

dotPoints.description: Select and use appropriate digital, visual, written and oral media to convey scientific arguments

prompts.question: DESCRIBE the most suitable medium for showing the slope map to residents, and why it suits this audience.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A Year 11 class has found that a steep slope beside a local road cracks and slumps after heavy rain. They have rainfall records, a sketch map of the slope and photographs of the cracks. They must present their findings to residents at a community meeting.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes a suitable medium for the slope map and explains why it suits residents as the audience
2 marks: Identifies a suitable medium, with a limited reason linked to the audience
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Name one medium and tie it to what the map has to show, such as where the cracks sit relative to the road.
Give a reason linked to residents: whether they can keep it, read it quickly or follow a spoken explanation.
commonStudentErrors: Choosing a medium without saying why it suits the residents.
Listing all four media types rather than selecting one that suits the audience and purpose.

sampleAnswers.answer: A visual map is more suitable than oral media alone because residents can see where the cracks sit on the slope in relation to the road at a glance. Its colours and labels show the scientific arguments about the slope without needing a reader to interpret tables. A printed map can also be kept by residents after the meeting, so it suits this audience well.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing a suitable visual map of the slope and explaining why it suits residents, who can read it at a glance and keep it.

sampleAnswers.answer: A printed map suits residents because they can see where the slope is.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying a suitable medium, with a limited reason linked to the residents. It does not explain how the map conveys the argument.

sampleAnswers.answer: The residents could read a written report about the slope.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by providing some relevant information. It names a medium but gives no reason it suits the audience.

prompts.question: ANALYSE the strengths and limitations of a graph of the rainfall data, compared with a written report, for presenting the scientific arguments to residents.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A Year 11 class has found that a steep slope beside a local road cracks and slumps after heavy rain. They have rainfall records, a sketch map of the slope and photographs of the cracks. They must present their findings to residents at a community meeting.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Analyses the strengths and limitations of the graph and the written report for these residents, using the rainfall and slope evidence
4 marks: Analyses the suitability of a graph or written report for residents, with relevant reference to the data
3 marks: Compares a graph and a written report, with some reasons for each
2 marks: Identifies a feature of a graph or written report, with limited reasons
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Compare both media on the same criteria, such as clarity for residents and how much scientific reasoning each can carry, rather than describing each one separately.
Refer to the rainfall data and the slope to show why a particular limitation matters for this meeting.
Finish with a judgement on the best medium or combination, supported by the reasons already given.
commonStudentErrors: Describing what a graph and a report look like without judging which suits the residents.
Saying a graph is better because it is visual, with no reference to the scientific arguments or the data.

sampleAnswers.answer: A graph of the rainfall data is a strong visual medium because residents can see the link between heavy rain and cracking on the slope at a glance. It is also easy to project at the meeting. Its limitation is that a graph shows the pattern but not the scientific arguments behind it, such as how saturated soil loses strength. A written report can explain that reasoning and the limits of the data, but many residents will not read it in time. The best choice is a graph supported by a short written summary, so residents see the pattern and understand the reasoning.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row by analysing the strengths and limitations of the graph and the written report for residents, using the rainfall and slope evidence, and reaching a judgement.

sampleAnswers.answer: A written report can explain the reasons for the slope movement, but residents may not read it. A graph shows the rainfall pattern clearly.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by comparing a graph and a written report, with a reason for each. It does not analyse their strengths and limitations in detail.

sampleAnswers.answer: Graphs are useful for showing data.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by providing some relevant information. It makes a general point about graphs and does not compare them with a report.

dotPoints.description: Apply appropriate scientific notations, language and nomenclature

prompts.question: DESCRIBE two changes that would correct the terms and notation used in this sentence.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A Year 11 student has written a lab report about a rock sample from a creek bed. One sentence reads: 'The rock was a hard stone made of tiny sparkly bits, mostly quartz written as SiO2, that came from squashing mud, and it had layers.'
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes two changes to the terms and notation, each with a sound reason from how the rock formed or what the formula shows
2 marks: Describes one correct change to the terms or notation, with a limited reason
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Correct the nomenclature and the notation separately: sedimentary rock and mineral grains for the terms, and a subscript 2 in the formula.
Give a reason for each change, such as sediment being compacted or the subscript showing the number of oxygen atoms in the formula.
commonStudentErrors: Replacing 'hard stone' with a vague word such as 'mineral' without naming the rock type.
Writing SiO2 with the 2 at normal size, which changes what the formula says.

sampleAnswers.answer: Two changes are needed. First, 'hard stone' should be replaced with the correct nomenclature, sedimentary rock, because the rock formed from compacted sediment, and 'tiny sparkly bits' should be described as mineral grains such as quartz. Second, the formula should follow scientific notation, with the 2 written as a subscript in SiO₂, because it shows two oxygen atoms for each silicon atom. This also keeps the wording in scientific language.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing two changes, the rock name and the formula notation, with a reason for each drawn from how the rock formed and what the formula shows.

sampleAnswers.answer: 'Hard stone' should be replaced with sedimentary rock, because the rock formed from sediment.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by describing one correct change to the terms, with a limited reason. The notation change is not made.

sampleAnswers.answer: The wording could be more formal and use the right words.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by providing some relevant information. It mentions wording but names no specific term or notation change.

prompts.question: APPLY correct nomenclature to rewrite the paragraph for a geology audience, naming the plate boundary described in each sentence.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student has written a paragraph for a geology newsletter. It reads: 'Where two plates bump and one goes under the other, the land rises into mountains. Where the plates slide past each other, the rock rubs and shakes. Where plates pull apart, the land goes up and new rock comes from below. The plates move at about 3 cms a year.'
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Applies correct nomenclature to all three plate boundaries and uses scientific notation and language to rewrite the paragraph
4 marks: Applies correct nomenclature to all three plate boundaries, with some correction of the wording or notation
3 marks: Names two plate boundaries correctly, with limited correction of the wording or notation
2 marks: Names one plate boundary correctly, with minimal reference to the paragraph
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Name all three boundary types and what happens at each, such as subduction at a convergent boundary, rather than describing plate movement in general.
Correct the notation and the wording together: the rate in cm yr⁻¹, and terms such as shearing or seismic activity in place of informal phrases.
Write for a geology audience, so precise terms are expected rather than explained in everyday words.
commonStudentErrors: Mixing up divergent and convergent boundaries, such as describing new crust forming where plates collide.
Changing only one word in the paragraph and leaving the rate written as cms a year.
Calling the transform boundary a mountain-building boundary.

sampleAnswers.answer: The paragraph should use correct nomenclature throughout. The first sentence describes a convergent boundary, where one plate subducts beneath another and forms mountains and volcanoes. The second describes a transform boundary, where plates slide past each other and cause earthquakes without creating new crust. The third describes a divergent boundary, where plates separate and magma rises to form new crust. Each boundary should be named once with its process stated, so the reader can follow the plate movement. The rate should use scientific notation as cm yr⁻¹, because unit symbols take no 's', and the informal 'rubs and shakes' should be replaced with scientific language such as shearing and seismic activity.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row by naming all three boundaries correctly, correcting the rate notation and replacing the informal wording with scientific language for a geology audience.

sampleAnswers.answer: The convergent boundary forms mountains, and the transform boundary is where plates slide past. The informal wording should be replaced with scientific language.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by naming two boundaries correctly and noting the need for scientific language. It does not name the divergent boundary or correct the rate notation.

sampleAnswers.answer: Plates can move apart, slide past each other or collide.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by providing some relevant information. It lists plate movements without naming the boundaries or correcting the paragraph.

dotPoints.description: Use evidence and correct scientific language and terminology to address a specific audience and purpose in a variety of contexts

prompts.question: DESCRIBE how the student could adjust the wording so that it suits this specific audience of Year 7 students while keeping the correct terminology.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A Year 11 student has written a science explanation of why a coastal rock platform is being worn away by waves. It uses the terms 'hydraulic action' and 'abrasion' and is intended for the school newsletter, which Year 7 students read.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes how to adjust the wording for Year 7 students while keeping the correct terminology, with a reason tied to the audience and purpose
2 marks: Identifies one suitable change to the wording, with limited reference to the audience
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Keep the correct terms and explain each in plain words suited to the audience, rather than replacing them with vague ones.
Tie each change to the purpose of the notice and to Year 7 readers, such as an example they can picture.
commonStudentErrors: Dropping the scientific terms altogether, so the explanation is no longer accurate.
Simplifying so much that the meaning changes, such as calling abrasion simply 'damage'.

sampleAnswers.answer: The student should keep the terminology 'hydraulic action' and 'abrasion' but explain each in plain words for this specific audience of Year 7 students, such as 'waves forcing air and water into cracks' and 'sand grinding the rock'. The notice should also include one piece of evidence, such as photographs of the platform changing over time, to support its purpose. This keeps the scientific language accurate while making it accessible.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing how the student keeps the correct terminology while explaining each term for Year 7 readers, with evidence linked to the purpose.

sampleAnswers.answer: The student could explain 'abrasion' in plainer words for Year 7 students.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying one suitable change, with limited reference to the audience. It does not show how the terminology stays accurate.

sampleAnswers.answer: The notice should be easier to read for younger students.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by providing some relevant information. It refers to the audience but names no change to the terminology.

prompts.question: ASSESS how well the journalist's draft uses scientific language and terminology for the specific audience of newspaper readers and its purpose of informing the community.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A science journalist is writing a feature for a local newspaper on a proposed seawall to protect a beach from wave erosion. The draft uses terms such as 'longshore drift', 'wave refraction' and 'hard engineering', and cites a local study of shoreline retreat as its evidence.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Assesses how well the draft's terminology, evidence and explanations suit the specific audience and purpose, with sustained reference to the text and a clear judgement
4 marks: Assesses how well the draft's terminology and evidence suit the audience, with relevant reference to its purpose
3 marks: Explains one strength or weakness of the draft's terminology for newspaper readers, with some relevant evidence
2 marks: Identifies a term from the draft and whether it suits readers, with limited explanation
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Judge the draft against its audience and purpose, not only whether the science is correct: is each term explained for general readers?
Use specific words from the draft, such as longshore drift, as evidence for each judgement.
Finish with an overall judgement on whether the draft meets its purpose, with reasons.
commonStudentErrors: Judging only whether the science is accurate, without considering the newspaper audience.
Saying the terminology is too hard without naming a term or explaining how it affects readers.

sampleAnswers.answer: The draft's terminology suits the specific audience only in part. Terms such as longshore drift and wave refraction are scientific language that general readers cannot follow, so each needs a brief plain definition at first use. The evidence is strongest where it links the shoreline study to this beach, but it does not say how the seawall would change the movement of sand along the coast. Hard engineering needs explaining too, and the article should set out its trade-offs. Overall the draft serves its purpose of informing the community, but the terminology and evidence need more explanation before it fully meets that purpose.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row by assessing how the terminology, evidence and explanations suit the specific audience and purpose, and reaching an overall judgement.

sampleAnswers.answer: The draft uses scientific language, but terms such as longshore drift need explaining for newspaper readers. The evidence is relevant to the beach.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining one weakness in the terminology, with a basic comment on the evidence. It does not assess how well the draft meets its purpose overall.

sampleAnswers.answer: The article should be easier for readers to understand.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by providing some relevant information. It makes a general point about readability without referring to the terminology or the evidence.

subTopics.name: Formation and structure of the Earth

dotPoints.description: Recognise Aboriginal Dreaming Stories and Torres Strait Islander Legends that feature the formation of the Earth

prompts.question: Describe how one Aboriginal Dreaming Story or Torres Strait Islander Legend explains the formation of the Earth.
prompts.scenario: Aboriginal Dreaming Stories and Torres Strait Islander Legends are Cultural Knowledge, held by the Peoples who tell them and passed on orally across generations. Many describe ancestral beings who shaped hills, rivers and waterholes, linking each feature to a particular place within Country.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes how a Dreaming Story or Legend explains the formation of the Earth, with relevant detail about the ancestral beings or landscape it describes
2 marks: Identifies one relevant way a Dreaming Story or Legend explains how the land was formed
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about Dreaming Stories or Torres Strait Islander Legends
markerNotes: Describe what the story says shaped the land, such as ancestral beings creating hills or waterways, in the story's own terms.
Name the Peoples or Nation the story belongs to where you can, which shows you recognise it as Cultural Knowledge.
Do not dismiss the story as a myth or judge it against science, because the mark is for describing its explanation.
commonStudentErrors: Calling the stories myths or fairy tales, which dismisses them instead of describing what they explain.
Writing about the science of plate tectonics rather than the formation described in the story.

sampleAnswers.answer: Aboriginal Dreaming Stories explain the formation of the Earth through ancestral beings who shaped hills, rivers and waterholes as they travelled across the land. As Cultural Knowledge, each feature is tied to a place within Country, so the story carries both the explanation and the knowledge of that place. A Torres Strait Islander Legend can explain the land in a similar way.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing how the stories explain formation, with specific features and a link to Country. It also treats the stories as Cultural Knowledge rather than dismissing them.

sampleAnswers.answer: Aboriginal Dreaming Stories explain how the land was formed by ancestral beings who shaped its features.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying one way a Dreaming Story explains formation. It gives no detail of the features shaped or of the link to Country, so it stays below the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Dreaming Stories are old stories told by Aboriginal Peoples.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by providing some relevant information about Dreaming Stories. It names no explanation of how the land was formed, so it does not reach the 2-mark row.

prompts.question: Discuss the place of Aboriginal Dreaming Stories and Torres Strait Islander Legends in understanding the formation of the Earth, alongside scientific explanations.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A Year 11 class is comparing a Dreaming Story about a landscape with a scientific account of the same land. Dreaming Stories are Cultural Knowledge passed down through generations and tied to Country, while scientific accounts are tested against evidence such as rock records and seismic data.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Discusses the place of Dreaming Stories and Legends as Cultural Knowledge, with sustained reasoning about how they sit alongside scientific explanations of the formation of the Earth
4 marks: Discusses clearly how Dreaming Stories and Legends hold knowledge about the formation of the Earth, with some reference to scientific explanations
3 marks: Describes how Dreaming Stories and Legends are Cultural Knowledge passed on through generations, with limited discussion of scientific evidence
2 marks: Identifies a relevant feature of Dreaming Stories or Legends, with little or no discussion
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about Dreaming Stories or Torres Strait Islander Legends
markerNotes: Reach a reasoned judgement about the place of the stories, not just a list of what they contain.
Use the scenario's contrast between Cultural Knowledge and tested evidence to show how each account is held and checked.
Show respect for both knowledge systems rather than calling the stories wrong because they are not science.
commonStudentErrors: Dismissing the Dreaming Stories as myths with no value, which is an unsupported judgement.
Describing the science of the Earth's formation in detail without discussing the Cultural Knowledge.
Listing features of the stories without giving reasons for their importance.

sampleAnswers.answer: Aboriginal Dreaming Stories and Torres Strait Islander Legends hold Cultural Knowledge about the formation of the Earth, and that knowledge has value in its own right. The stories are passed on orally across generations and link the land to Country, to its people and to their responsibilities for it. Scientific explanations are also valuable because they rest on evidence such as rock records and seismic data, which can be tested and revised. The two accounts answer different questions. The stories explain how the land is connected to people and to ancestral beings, while science explains the physical processes that shaped it. Recognising both gives a fuller understanding of the Earth, and the stories deserve respect rather than being judged wrong because they are not science.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row by discussing the stories as Cultural Knowledge and how they sit alongside scientific explanations, with reasons drawn from the evidence each account rests on. The judgement about respect for both systems is supported rather than asserted.

sampleAnswers.answer: Dreaming Stories and Legends are Cultural Knowledge passed on through generations, so they carry knowledge about the land. Science also explains how the Earth formed, using evidence such as rock records, so the two accounts can sit side by side.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing the stories as Cultural Knowledge passed through generations, with a brief reference to scientific evidence. It does not discuss how the two accounts relate or give reasons for their value, so it stays below the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Aboriginal Dreaming Stories are old stories about the land.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by providing some relevant information about the stories. It gives no reason for their value and no link to scientific accounts, so it stays at the bottom row.

dotPoints.description: Use accretion theory and the concept of the ‘potato radius’ to account for the formation and shape of the Earth and smaller celestial bodies

prompts.question: Describe the concept of the potato radius and what it implies for the shape of smaller celestial bodies.
prompts.scenario: Accretion theory holds that the Earth and other bodies grew from dust and rock that collided and stuck together under gravity. The potato radius is the size below which a body's gravity is too weak to round it, so smaller bodies can remain irregular in shape.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes the potato radius as the size threshold below which a body stays irregular and above which gravity rounds it, with a link to accretion theory
2 marks: Describes the potato radius or accretion theory with some link to the shape of a celestial body
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the shape of a celestial body
markerNotes: Define the potato radius as a size threshold, then say what happens to shape on each side of it.
Link the shape to gravity and to the internal strength of the rock, not just to size.
Mention accretion theory as the process by which these bodies grew.
commonStudentErrors: Saying the potato radius is a fixed name for a shape rather than a size at which gravity takes over.
Stating that small bodies are irregular because they are small, without explaining the role of gravity.

sampleAnswers.answer: The potato radius is the size below which a body's gravity is too weak to overcome the strength of its rock, so it stays irregular in shape. Above this size, gravity pulls material towards the centre and rounds the body. Accretion theory explains how these bodies grew from collisions, so smaller celestial bodies such as many asteroids keep irregular shapes.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by defining the potato radius as a size threshold, explaining what gravity does above it, and linking this to accretion theory. The reasoning about rock strength makes the link to shape specific.

sampleAnswers.answer: The potato radius is a size threshold, and smaller bodies stay irregular in shape.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by describing the potato radius as a size threshold linked to shape. It does not explain why gravity rounds larger bodies, so it stays below the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Small asteroids are less round than the Earth.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by providing some relevant information about shape. It does not describe the potato radius or accretion theory, so it does not reach the 2-mark row.

prompts.question: Justify why the Earth is nearly spherical while many small asteroids are irregular, using the potato radius and accretion theory.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: Two students compare a photograph of the Earth from space with an image of a small asteroid shaped like a lumpy rock. They want to explain the difference using accretion theory and gravity.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Justifies with sustained reasoning why gravity rounds a body above the potato radius but leaves a smaller body irregular, linked to accretion theory
5 marks: Justifies clearly why size determines shape, using the potato radius and accretion theory with some depth
4 marks: Explains the link between gravity and shape using the potato radius, with some reasoning
3 marks: Describes the potato radius or accretion theory, with limited reasoning about the Earth or asteroids
2 marks: Identifies a relevant feature of the Earth or asteroids with little explanation
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about shape or gravity
markerNotes: Make a reasoned claim about why size matters, then support it with the potato radius and the role of gravity.
Use accretion theory to explain how the bodies grew, rather than stating only that the Earth is round.
Place each body on one side or the other of the potato radius, and say what that means for its shape.
commonStudentErrors: Saying the Earth is round because it rotates, without linking shape to gravity or the potato radius.
Treating all asteroids as one group, without distinguishing those below the potato radius from larger bodies.

sampleAnswers.answer: A body's shape depends mainly on its size, because gravity can reshape a body only if it is large enough for its own pull to overcome the strength of its rock. Under accretion theory, the Earth grew by collisions between smaller particles and rock, and as it grew its gravity increased. Once a body is larger than the potato radius, its gravity is strong enough to overcome the internal strength of its rock, so material is pulled towards the centre and the body becomes nearly spherical. This is why the Earth is round. Many small asteroids lie below the potato radius. Their gravity is too weak to overcome the strength of their rock, so they keep irregular, lumpy shapes set during their formation. The same explanation accounts for both the nearly spherical Earth and the irregular asteroids, so the difference reflects size and gravity rather than a special property of the Earth.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by justifying, with sustained reasoning, why gravity rounds a body above the potato radius and leaves a smaller one irregular. The reasoning is tied to accretion theory and to the strength of rock throughout.

sampleAnswers.answer: Small asteroids stay irregular because they are small, while the Earth is round because it is large. The potato radius is the size at which shape begins to change.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing the potato radius and linking it to shape, with limited reasoning about the Earth and asteroids. It does not explain the role of gravity or the internal strength of rock, so it stays below the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The Earth is round and asteroids are not.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by providing some relevant information about shape. It gives no link to gravity, the potato radius or accretion theory, so it does not reach the 2-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Conduct a laboratory experiment to model the hypothesised role of density separation in planetary differentiation

prompts.question: Explain why the iron filings collected at the bottom of the container, and how this laboratory experiment models planetary differentiation.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student places a mixture of iron filings, sand and small plastic beads in a tall clear container of water. After shaking the container and leaving it to settle, the iron filings are at the bottom, the sand forms a layer above them and the plastic beads float at the top.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Explains why the denser iron filings sink through density separation and links this clearly to planetary differentiation
3 marks: Explains the role of density in why the iron filings settle, with some link to planetary differentiation
2 marks: Describes what happens in the container, with limited explanation of density
1 mark: Identifies a relevant observation from the container
markerNotes: Give the cause: density decides where each material settles, so the reason must be stated in terms of density.
Link the container to the Earth explicitly, saying that the dense iron sinking to the centre models the core forming.
Name the simplification in the model when you are asked how it models the Earth.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the layers without saying that density causes the iron filings to settle at the bottom.
Saying the iron filings are heavy rather than denser than the other materials.

sampleAnswers.answer: In this laboratory experiment, the iron filings are denser than the water, sand and plastic beads, so they sink through the water and settle at the bottom. This is density separation: materials sort themselves by density, with the densest material lowest. The student's model suggests that in the early Earth, molten iron-rich material sank towards the centre to form the core, while lighter silicate material rose to form the mantle and crust. That is planetary differentiation. The container is a simplified model, however, because the real process happened at far higher temperatures and pressures.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row by explaining the settling through density separation and linking it clearly to planetary differentiation. It also states the limitation of the model, which keeps the answer accurate.

sampleAnswers.answer: The iron filings settle at the bottom because they are the densest material in the container. The sand forms a middle layer.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by describing the layers and giving a basic density reason. It does not link the result to the early Earth, so it stays below the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The iron filings went to the bottom.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying an observation from the container. It gives no explanation of density, so it does not reach the 2-mark row.

prompts.question: Assess the validity of this laboratory experiment as a model of planetary differentiation in the early Earth.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: The same container of iron filings, sand and plastic beads is used by a Year 11 class as a model of the early Earth. Students must judge how far the model reflects real planetary processes.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Assesses the validity of the experiment with sustained reasoning, weighing its strengths and at least two specific limitations
5 marks: Assesses the validity of the experiment with clear reasoning and at least one specific limitation
4 marks: Assesses the experiment with some reasoning, identifying a strength and a limitation
3 marks: Describes the model and makes a limited judgement about its usefulness
2 marks: Identifies a relevant feature of the experiment with little judgement
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about density or the early Earth
markerNotes: Weigh the model's strengths and its limitations before reaching a judgement on validity.
Name a specific limitation, such as pressure at depth or the materials used, rather than saying the model is simply not perfect.
Finish with a clear judgement about what the model can and cannot show.
commonStudentErrors: Saying the model is valid because it looks like the Earth, without testing it against the real processes.
Listing limitations with no judgement of how much they affect the model's validity.

sampleAnswers.answer: The laboratory experiment is a valid model of density separation, because the iron filings, sand and plastic beads sort into layers by density, in the same way that molten material in the early Earth is thought to have separated into core, mantle and crust. This gives the model real value for showing the principle of planetary differentiation. Its validity has several limitations, however. The early Earth was hot enough for rock to melt and flow over long periods, whereas the container is cool and the materials settle within minutes. The model also uses a few arbitrary materials, while the Earth contained many elements that behaved differently under heat and pressure. Pressure is the most serious limitation: it increases greatly with depth inside a planet, which the model cannot reproduce. A fair judgement is that the experiment is useful for teaching density separation, but it cannot test the actual process in the early Earth.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by weighing the model's strengths against several specific limitations, with pressure at depth identified as the most serious. The conclusion states exactly what the model can and cannot show.

sampleAnswers.answer: The container shows density separation, where the iron filings sink and the plastic beads float. It is a useful model, but it is not exact.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing the model and making a limited judgement that it is useful. It names no specific limitation, so it stays below the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The samples differ in their density.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by providing some relevant information about density. It makes no judgement of validity and names no pair of materials, so it does not reach the 2-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Outline the processes that initially formed the geosphere, atmosphere and hydrosphere

prompts.question: Outline how the atmosphere and hydrosphere formed as the molten Earth cooled, and how the geosphere solidified at the surface.
prompts.scenario: The early Earth was largely molten after accretion, and its surface cooled over time. Scientists explain the formation of the geosphere, atmosphere and hydrosphere through processes such as outgassing and condensation.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Outlines the processes that formed the early atmosphere and hydrosphere as the surface cooled, with a clear link to the geosphere
2 marks: Identifies a relevant process or two that formed part of the early Earth, with limited detail
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the early Earth or its atmosphere
markerNotes: Outline each process in one or two sentences, saying what it produced, such as the atmosphere or the hydrosphere.
Include the cooling of the surface, because it is what allows water vapour to condense and the geosphere to solidify.
Name the geosphere's solid surface as the first layer to form, so the answer covers all three spheres.
commonStudentErrors: Naming a process without saying what it formed, such as writing outgassing without linking it to the atmosphere.
Describing the Earth today, such as its oceans and air, rather than how they first formed.

sampleAnswers.answer: As the molten Earth cooled, its surface solidified to form the geosphere. Volcanic outgassing released water vapour and gases such as carbon dioxide, which built up the early atmosphere. Once the surface cooled below boiling point, condensation of this water vapour produced rain that filled low areas to form the hydrosphere. These processes built the Earth's first surface layers over long periods.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by outlining the processes of outgassing and condensation as the surface cooled, with a clear link to the geosphere. Each process is tied to what it produced.

sampleAnswers.answer: Volcanic outgassing released gases that formed the early atmosphere. Rain then filled the oceans.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying outgassing and rain as processes that formed part of the early Earth. It does not explain the cooling that made condensation possible, so it stays below the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The early Earth had gases in its atmosphere.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by providing some relevant information about the early atmosphere. It names no process, so it does not reach the 2-mark row.

prompts.question: Analyse how the cooling of the molten early Earth connected the formation of its geosphere, atmosphere and hydrosphere.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A Year 11 student claims the oceans formed before the early atmosphere. The student's view does not account for the water vapour released by outgassing, or for how condensation of that vapour formed the oceans.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Analyses how cooling linked the formation of the geosphere, atmosphere and hydrosphere, with clear cause and effect and specific processes
4 marks: Analyses the processes of outgassing and condensation with some link to cooling and the three spheres
3 marks: Explains a process that formed part of the early Earth, with limited link to cooling and the other spheres
2 marks: Identifies a relevant process or feature of the early Earth with little explanation
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the early Earth or its surface
markerNotes: Trace the chain of cause and effect: cooling allowed solidification and condensation, and condensation formed the oceans.
Name the specific processes, outgassing and condensation, rather than writing about the early Earth in general.
Show the dependence between the spheres, such as the hydrosphere depending on water vapour from the atmosphere.
commonStudentErrors: Listing the three spheres in order without saying how cooling connected them.
Stating that the oceans came from the atmosphere without naming condensation as the process.

sampleAnswers.answer: As the molten early Earth cooled, its outer surface solidified first to form the geosphere, a thin crust over hotter material below. Outgassing from volcanoes released water vapour and other gases, which built up the atmosphere. Once the surface cooled below boiling point, condensation of this water vapour produced rain over a very long period, filling the low areas to form the hydrosphere. Cooling therefore linked all three spheres: it allowed the surface to solidify, and it allowed the water vapour from outgassing to condense rather than remain as steam. The hydrosphere depended on the atmosphere, because the oceans could only form once the water vapour in the atmosphere condensed.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row by analysing cooling as the link between the three spheres, with each step given as a cause and effect. The dependence of the hydrosphere on the atmosphere is explained rather than asserted.

sampleAnswers.answer: Outgassing released water vapour and gases into the early atmosphere. When the Earth cooled, condensation of the water vapour produced rain that formed the hydrosphere.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining outgassing and condensation, with a basic link to cooling. It does not show how the geosphere, atmosphere and hydrosphere depend on each other, so it stays below the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The early Earth had a hot surface.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by providing some relevant information about the early Earth. It names no process and no link to cooling, so it stays at the bottom row.

dotPoints.description: Use Lehmann’s seismic wave methodology to provide evidence for the internal structure of the Earth

prompts.question: Explain why S-waves are absent from the shadow zone on the far side of the Earth from an earthquake, and what this shows about the outer core.
prompts.scenario: Seismic waves from an earthquake travel through the Earth and are recorded at stations around the world. S-waves travel only through solids, while P-waves can travel through both solids and liquids.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Explains why S-waves are absent from the shadow zone and what this shows about the outer core, with reference to seismic evidence
2 marks: Describes the absence of S-waves in the shadow zone without explaining why
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about seismic waves or the Earth's interior
markerNotes: Give the reason: S-waves do not travel through liquid, so the liquid outer core stops them.
State the conclusion the absence supports, which is that the outer core is liquid.
Connect the evidence to Lehmann's method of reading seismic records, so the answer shows how the evidence was used.
commonStudentErrors: Saying S-waves are blocked by the core without saying that the outer core is liquid.
Confusing S-waves with P-waves and stating that both are absent from the shadow zone.

sampleAnswers.answer: S-waves cannot travel through liquid, so they do not pass through the outer core and are absent from the shadow zone on the far side of the Earth. This absence shows that the outer core is liquid. The seismic wave methodology used by Lehmann relies on such records, which contribute to our understanding of the internal structure of the Earth.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining the absence of S-waves through the liquid outer core and stating what this shows. The reference to Lehmann's methodology ties the evidence to the internal structure of the Earth.

sampleAnswers.answer: S-waves are missing on the far side of the Earth from the earthquake.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by describing the absence of S-waves in the shadow zone. It gives no reason for the absence and says nothing about the outer core, so it stays below the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Seismic waves are used to study the Earth.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by providing some relevant information about seismic waves. It does not describe the shadow zone or the outer core, so it does not reach the 2-mark row.

prompts.question: Analyse why unexpected P-wave arrivals in the shadow zone led Lehmann to infer a solid inner core.
prompts.scenario: Seismologists record the arrival times of P-waves from distant earthquakes at stations around the world. Earlier models assumed the whole core was liquid, so P-waves were expected to be absent from the shadow zone, which makes the unexpected evidence there hard to explain.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Analyses how Lehmann's methodology and the unexpected P-wave arrivals led to the inference of a solid inner core, with clear reasoning throughout
4 marks: Analyses the unexpected P-wave arrivals in the shadow zone and links them to the internal structure of the Earth
3 marks: Explains the role of P-waves or seismic evidence in revealing layers of the Earth, with limited analysis
2 marks: Identifies a relevant seismic feature or layer of the Earth with little explanation
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about seismic waves or the Earth's layers
markerNotes: Set out the expectation first, then the surprise, then the inference, so each step of the reasoning is visible.
Use the terms P-waves and shadow zone precisely, and say what the arrivals showed.
Explain what the inference means for the internal structure of the Earth, not just that the finding was important.
commonStudentErrors: Saying Lehmann discovered the core without explaining the P-wave evidence that led to the inference.
Describing S-waves as the evidence for the inner core, when the inner core result depends on P-waves.

sampleAnswers.answer: Lehmann's seismic wave methodology compared the arrival times of P-waves recorded at stations after distant earthquakes. Earlier models predicted that P-waves would be absent from the shadow zone, but Lehmann found unexpected P-wave arrivals there. These arrivals were best explained if the waves had been refracted or reflected by a dense solid layer at the centre of the Earth. Lehmann therefore inferred a solid inner core within the liquid outer core, which accounts for the evidence. This finding is an important part of the internal structure of the Earth, showing how seismic records can reveal layers that cannot be sampled directly.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row by analysing the expectation, the unexpected arrivals and the inference in sequence. Each step is explained, and the finding is connected to the internal structure of the Earth.

sampleAnswers.answer: P-waves were found in the shadow zone, where they were not expected. This suggests the Earth has a solid layer at its centre that bends the waves.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining why the P-wave arrivals matter for the Earth's layers. It does not analyse the reasoning in depth or name the inner core, so it stays below the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Seismic waves travel through the Earth.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by providing some relevant information about seismic waves. It names no feature of the internal structure, so it does not reach the 2-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Conduct a practical investigation to model the processes of seismic wave reflection and refraction inside the Earth

prompts.question: Explain why the ripples bend at the sloping boundary in this practical investigation, and what happens to the part of each ripple that bounces back.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student uses a ripple tray to model seismic waves in a practical investigation. One section of the tray is deep, the other shallow, and a sloping boundary joins them. The ripples slow down in the shallow section, and the change in speed is what the student compares with waves inside the Earth.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Explains refraction and reflection at the boundary in the model, linking the change in speed to what happens inside the Earth
3 marks: Explains refraction or reflection at the boundary, with some link to the layers of the Earth
2 marks: Describes what the ripples do at the boundary with limited explanation
1 mark: Identifies a relevant observation from the model
markerNotes: Give the cause: a change in speed at the boundary, which then changes the direction of travel (refraction).
Name both effects, refraction and reflection, and say what each does to the wave.
Link the model to the Earth by naming the layer boundary that seismic waves cross.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the bend without saying that the speed of the ripples changes at the boundary.
Calling the bounce-back refraction, when the reflected part of the wave stays in the same material.

sampleAnswers.answer: In this practical investigation, the ripples bend at the sloping boundary because they slow down in the shallow section. As the speed changes, the direction of travel changes too, which is refraction. Part of each ripple is also sent back into the deep section, which is seismic wave reflection. Inside the Earth, seismic waves behave in a similar way when they meet a boundary between layers with different properties, so the model helps explain how waves reveal structure inside the Earth.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row by explaining both refraction and reflection at the boundary, linking the change in speed to the behaviour of seismic waves inside the Earth.

sampleAnswers.answer: The ripples bend at the boundary and part of each ripple bounces back.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by describing what the ripples do at the boundary. It does not explain why they bend or link the model to the Earth, so it stays below the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The ripples cross the boundary.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying an observation from the model. It gives no explanation of the bending or the bounce, so it does not reach the 2-mark row.

prompts.question: Assess the validity of this practical investigation as a model of seismic wave reflection and refraction inside the Earth, including at least two limitations.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A Year 11 class uses a ripple tray with a sloping boundary to model seismic waves. The ripples bend and partly reflect at the boundary, but the tray uses water in two dimensions rather than rock in the Earth.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Assesses the validity of the model with sustained reasoning, weighing its strengths and at least two specific limitations
5 marks: Assesses the model's validity with clear reasoning and at least one specific limitation
4 marks: Assesses the model with some reasoning, identifying a strength and a limitation
3 marks: Describes what the model shows about refraction or reflection, with a limited judgement of its validity
2 marks: Identifies a relevant feature of the model or of seismic waves with little judgement
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about seismic waves or the practical model
markerNotes: Judge the model against the real processes: which physics it reproduces and which features of the Earth it cannot.
Name at least two specific limitations, such as surface waves in two dimensions or a single material, and explain why each matters.
Finish with a clear overall judgement of validity, such as valid for one process but not for the full structure.
commonStudentErrors: Saying the model is valid because it looks like the Earth, without testing its physics.
Listing limitations without saying how much they reduce the validity of the model.

sampleAnswers.answer: The practical investigation is a valid model of the physics of seismic wave reflection and refraction, because the ripples slow in the shallow section, bend at the boundary and partly reflect back, as seismic waves do when they meet a boundary inside the Earth. The model is therefore useful for teaching how wave behaviour depends on speed. Its validity has clear limitations, however. Water ripples are surface waves in two dimensions, whereas seismic waves are body waves that travel through the whole three-dimensional Earth, so the tray cannot show waves passing through the interior. The tray also uses one material, water, while the Earth has many layers with different properties and pressures. Finally, the tray cannot reproduce the shadow zones that real seismic records reveal. Overall, the model is valid for the basic physics of refraction and reflection, but not for the full structure inside the Earth.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by weighing the model's strengths against specific limitations, namely the two-dimensional surface waves and the single material. The overall judgement states what the model is valid for.

sampleAnswers.answer: The ripples slow in the shallow part and bend at the boundary, which shows refraction. It is a useful model, but it is not completely accurate.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing refraction in the tray with a limited judgement of its usefulness. It names no specific limitation, so it stays below the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Ripples are waves on water.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by providing some relevant information about the practical model. It describes no refraction or reflection and makes no judgement, so it does not reach the 2-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Describe the relative thickness, temperature and physical properties of the asthenosphere, crust, lithosphere, outer core and inner core

prompts.question: Describe how the crust, the outer core and the inner core differ in relative thickness, temperature and physical properties.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student is labelling a diagram of the Earth's interior for a class poster. Seismic evidence shows that the crust is the outermost and thinnest layer, while the cores lie far below the surface.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes the relative thickness, temperature and physical properties of all three layers accurately, with a clear comparison between them
2 marks: Describes some of the thickness, temperature or physical properties of the layers, with limited comparison
1 mark: Identifies one relevant feature of the crust or the cores
markerNotes: Cover each of the three named layers, comparing them on thickness, temperature and physical state.
Give the reason the inner core is solid despite its high temperature, which is the enormous pressure at the centre.
commonStudentErrors: Saying the inner core is liquid because it is the hottest layer.
Describing only one property of each layer, such as location, rather than thickness, temperature and physical properties.

sampleAnswers.answer: In relative thickness, the crust is the thinnest layer, far thinner than either core. The outer core is much thicker than the inner core. In temperature, the inner core is hotter than the outer core, which is hotter than the mantle. In physical properties, the outer core is liquid, while the inner core is solid because of the enormous pressure at the centre.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing relative thickness, temperature and physical properties for all three layers, with a clear comparison between them. The reason the inner core is solid is given.

sampleAnswers.answer: The outer core is liquid and the inner core is solid. The crust is the thinnest layer.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by describing the physical properties of the cores and the thickness of the crust. It gives no temperatures and no comparison between the layers, so it stays below the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The inner core is at the centre of the Earth.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying a relevant feature of the cores. It gives no description of thickness, temperature or physical properties, so it does not reach the 2-mark row.

prompts.question: Distinguish between the lithosphere and the asthenosphere in terms of their temperature and physical properties.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student says that the lithosphere and the asthenosphere are both solid rock at a similar temperature, so they must behave in the same way. The student's view ignores how the rock changes with depth.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Distinguishes clearly between the lithosphere and asthenosphere in temperature and physical properties, with a reasoned link to plate movement
4 marks: Distinguishes the two layers in temperature and physical properties, with some explanation of their behaviour
3 marks: Describes the temperature or physical properties of one layer, with a limited contrast to the other
2 marks: Identifies a relevant feature of the lithosphere or asthenosphere with little comparison
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the lithosphere or asthenosphere
markerNotes: Contrast the two layers on each property in turn: temperature, then rigidity or flow.
Explain the consequence of the difference, such as plates moving over the asthenosphere.
Say directly whether the student's view is correct, and why.
commonStudentErrors: Saying both layers are solid rock at similar temperatures, which is the misconception the scenario sets up.
Describing the lithosphere alone and never stating how the asthenosphere differs.

sampleAnswers.answer: The lithosphere and the asthenosphere differ in both temperature and physical properties. The lithosphere is the cool, rigid outer layer, made of the crust and the uppermost mantle. It is brittle, so it breaks and causes earthquakes when it deforms. The asthenosphere lies beneath it in the upper mantle and is hotter. Its rock is partly soft or plastic, so it deforms slowly and can flow over long periods even though it remains solid. This difference matters because the rigid lithosphere moves as plates over the weaker asthenosphere. The student's view is therefore incorrect: the two layers differ in temperature and behaviour.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row by distinguishing the two layers on temperature and on physical properties, with a reasoned link to plate movement. The student's view is judged directly and supported.

sampleAnswers.answer: The lithosphere is a rigid layer near the surface, and the asthenosphere is beneath it.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by describing the lithosphere with a limited contrast to the asthenosphere. It gives no temperature or physical property for the asthenosphere, so it stays below the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The asthenosphere is part of the mantle.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by providing some relevant information about the asthenosphere. It makes no comparison and gives no temperature or physical property, so it does not reach the 2-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Conduct a laboratory experiment to compare the density of samples representing oceanic crust, continental crust, mantle and core, using quantitative data

prompts.question: Classify the four samples from least to most dense, and explain why the continental crust sample is the least dense.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student has four samples representing oceanic crust, continental crust, mantle and core. In a laboratory experiment using quantitative data, the student finds that the continental crust sample is the least dense and the core sample is the densest.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Classifies all four samples in the correct order of density and explains the continental crust result using composition
2 marks: Classifies the samples in part, correctly placing at least the least and most dense samples
1 mark: Identifies one relevant sample or density difference
markerNotes: Give the full order from least to most dense, not just the two extremes.
Link the order to composition: continental crust is richer in lighter minerals, while the core is mostly iron and nickel.
commonStudentErrors: Placing oceanic crust below continental crust, which reverses the density order.
Giving the order without any reason based on composition.

sampleAnswers.answer: In this laboratory experiment, the order of density from least to most is continental crust, oceanic crust, mantle, then core. The quantitative data show that continental crust is the least dense because it is richer in lighter, silica-rich minerals than oceanic crust. The core is the densest because it is mostly iron and nickel, which are much denser than rock.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by placing all four samples in the correct order of density and explaining the continental crust result using composition. The reason for the core's density is also given.

sampleAnswers.answer: Continental crust is the least dense sample and the core is the densest.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by correctly placing the least and most dense samples. It does not order the oceanic crust and mantle or give a composition reason, so it stays below the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The core is denser than the mantle.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying one correct density difference between two samples. It does not place the least or most dense sample, so it does not reach the 2-mark row.

prompts.question: Assess the validity of using these small laboratory samples to represent the density of the mantle and the core.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student tests small samples of oceanic crust, continental crust, a mantle rock and an iron-nickel metal standing in for the core. The student reports density comparisons from quantitative data collected in the laboratory experiment.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Assesses the validity of the samples as stand-ins for the mantle and core with sustained reasoning and at least two specific limitations
5 marks: Assesses the validity of the samples with clear reasoning and at least one specific limitation for the mantle or core
4 marks: Assesses the comparison with some reasoning, identifying a strength and a limitation
3 marks: Describes the density comparison between the samples with a limited judgement of its validity
2 marks: Identifies a relevant density difference between two samples with little judgement
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about density, samples or the Earth's layers
markerNotes: Separate what the samples can show, the relative density order, from what they cannot, the true density of the mantle and core.
Name at least two specific limitations, such as sample representativeness, pressure and temperature, and explain their effect.
Finish with a judgement on validity that is limited to what the method can show.
commonStudentErrors: Saying the samples are valid because the results were measured, without testing whether they represent the layers.
Listing limitations without explaining how they affect the density values.

sampleAnswers.answer: The laboratory experiment is useful because it shows the relative order of density: continental crust is less dense than oceanic crust, and both are less dense than the mantle and core. The quantitative data are consistent and repeatable, which supports the comparison between the samples. However, using small samples to represent the mantle and core has serious limitations. Mantle rock reaches the surface only rarely, so a sample may not be typical of the whole layer. The core cannot be sampled at all, so the iron-nickel metal is only a stand-in and is held at far lower pressure than the real core. Density also depends on temperature and pressure, which a small sample at room conditions cannot reproduce. Seismic and meteorite evidence are therefore needed to support the density values. The samples are valid for comparing relative density, but not for measuring the true density of the mantle and core.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by separating what the samples can show from what they cannot. Several specific limitations, including sample representativeness and pressure, are explained in terms of their effect on the density values.

sampleAnswers.answer: The results show that the core sample is the densest and the continental crust sample is the least dense. The comparison is useful for seeing the main pattern.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing the density comparison with a limited judgement that it is useful. It names no specific limitation of the samples, so it stays below the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The samples differ in their density.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by giving relevant information about density. It makes no judgement of validity and names no pair of samples, so it does not reach the 2-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Explain how the composition and density of meteorites provides evidence for the Earth’s composition

prompts.question: Compare the composition and density of iron meteorites with stony meteorites.
prompts.scenario: Meteorites are rocks from space that reach the Earth's surface. Scientists study their composition and density to learn about the materials that formed planetary bodies, including the Earth.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Compares the composition and density of both meteorite types and links the result to the composition of planetary bodies
2 marks: Compares one feature of the two meteorite types with limited reference to planetary composition
1 mark: Identifies a relevant feature of iron or stony meteorites
markerNotes: Compare both meteorite types on composition and on density, using the same features for each.
Link the difference to planetary composition, such as the metal core and silicate mantle.
commonStudentErrors: Describing only iron meteorites and not making a comparison with stony meteorites.
Saying stony meteorites are denser than iron meteorites, which reverses the density difference.

sampleAnswers.answer: Iron meteorites are mostly iron and nickel metal and have a high density, while stony meteorites are made mainly of silicate minerals and have a lower density. Iron meteorites are thought to come from the metal cores of planetary bodies that separated by density, which is evidence that dense metal can form a core. The lower density of stony meteorites is consistent with the silicate composition of the mantle and crust.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by comparing the composition and density of both types and linking the result to the composition of planetary bodies. The reference to cores and mantle makes the link explicit.
