1 mark: Provides some relevant information about extraction techniques
markerNotes: Sustained evaluation weighs the drawbacks of each technique against the features of its specific location.
Judgements must draw on the scenario, such as depth, setting and risk, and reach a conclusion for each project.
Treat each project separately before comparing them, so that no project is passed over.
commonStudentErrors: Describing each technique without judging whether it suits its location.
Treating the four projects as one case, rather than matching each technique to its own location.
Declaring one technique the best overall without reasons drawn from the scenario.

sampleAnswers.answer: Open pit mining suits the gold project because the ore lies in a wide layer near the surface, so the machinery can reach it directly from the surface. The arid location limits water, so dust control and water recycling are the main environmental issues to manage, and the large volume of waste rock must be stored safely. The copper vein lies at depth beneath farmland, so underground mining is the only practical one of the extraction techniques there. It leaves the surface largely intact, which protects the farmland and the town, although ventilation, ground stability and the cost of tunnelling are real drawbacks. Offshore drilling for gas under the continental shelf suits its location, because the reservoir lies beneath the seabed and a platform reaches it without disturbing land. Its risks are spills and damage to marine ecosystems, and these must be weighed against the lack of land use. Onshore drilling beneath the national park is poorly suited to its location: wells, roads and pipelines fragment habitat, and any leak threatens protected ecosystems. Onshore drilling would suit cleared farmland far better. Overall, each technique suits its location only when its risks can be controlled, and open pit mining and offshore drilling are the strongest matches for their projects.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 7-8 row by weighing each technique against the features of its location, with a supported judgement for all four projects.

sampleAnswers.answer: Open pit mining suits the gold project because the ore is near the surface, but the arid location makes dust and water management important. Underground mining suits the copper vein at depth, and it protects the farmland, although tunnelling is costly. Onshore drilling in a national park is poorly suited because wells and roads fragment habitat.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row by assessing the techniques for most projects with relevant reasons, but the judgement of suitability is brief.

sampleAnswers.answer: Open pit mining is used for the gold mine, and offshore drilling is used for gas.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies one technique for one project, without any evaluation of how well it suits the location.

dotPoints.description: Assess practices used by mining companies to minimise environmental impact

prompts.question: DESCRIBE two practices a mining company could use to reduce the dust and runoff from a new mine, and the environmental impact that each practice reduces.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A company plans a new open pit mine beside a creek. Residents are concerned about dust blown from the haul roads and stockpiles, and about rainwater running off the disturbed ground into the creek.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes two specific practices, each linked to the environmental impact it reduces, such as sealed haul roads for dust or sediment ponds for runoff
2 marks: Describes one relevant practice, or names two practices without explaining the impact each one reduces
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about reducing the impact of mining
markerNotes: Name a specific practice, such as sealed roads or sediment ponds, rather than a general aim such as being environmentally responsible.
Each practice needs its own impact, so check that the link to dust or runoff is stated for both.
commonStudentErrors: Naming practices, such as rehabilitation, without saying which impact each one reduces.
Describing the impact of the mine rather than a practice used to minimise it.

sampleAnswers.answer: Mining companies can water or seal the haul roads, which helps minimise dust blowing onto nearby homes and the creek, so the air-quality impact is reduced. They can also build sediment ponds around the disturbed ground, which traps runoff so that soil and chemicals do not reach the creek. These practices reduce the environmental impact on water quality.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing two specific practices and linking each to the impact it reduces, dust for the roads and runoff for the ponds.

sampleAnswers.answer: The company can water the haul roads and build sediment ponds.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by naming two practices without explaining the impact each one reduces.

sampleAnswers.answer: Mining companies can try to reduce their impact on the environment.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Provides some relevant information, but names no specific practice.

prompts.question: JUSTIFY which of progressive rehabilitation or sediment control is the more effective practice for minimising the environmental impact of a mine beside a creek.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A mining company operates a coal mine on a catchment that feeds a creek. Its plan rehabilitates each section of the mine as soon as digging is finished, and routes runoff through sediment ponds before it reaches the creek. Some residents argue that the ponds miss the finest clay particles and that rehabilitation takes decades to become fully effective.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Justifies a judgement on which practice is more effective, weighing how each addresses the impact at source or in runoff, its limitations and its timescale, with reasons clearly linked to the creek
5 marks: Justifies a judgement with relevant reasons for both practices, comparing their effectiveness and linking at least one reason to the creek
4 marks: Justifies a choice with some relevant reasons, with limited comparison of the two practices
3 marks: Describes the two practices and some features of each, with a basic link to the creek
2 marks: Identifies one practice or one feature of the impact, without a justified choice
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about mine practices
markerNotes: Progressive rehabilitation works at the source by stopping erosion, while sediment ponds treat runoff after it has formed; a strong answer uses that difference.
A justified choice names the limitation of the chosen practice, such as the timescale or the finest particles, and why it is still the better option.
commonStudentErrors: Choosing a practice without giving reasons, or saying both are equally good with no judgement.
Treating sediment ponds as a complete solution, without noting that the finest clay particles can pass through them.

sampleAnswers.answer: Progressive rehabilitation is the more effective practice for most of the mine's life, because it treats the source of the impact. Once each section is finished, reshaping and revegetating the ground stops erosion, so less sediment is produced in the first place. Mining companies that rehabilitate progressively therefore minimise the environmental impact on the creek across the whole catchment. Sediment control is a different kind of practice: sediment ponds treat runoff only after it has formed, and they miss the finest clay particles that some residents describe. Each of these practices has a role, but the two practices differ in when they act. Rehabilitation has its own limitation, since the vegetation takes decades to become fully effective, so the creek is exposed during that time and sediment control is still needed during active mining. However, the practice that protects the creek over the long term is progressive rehabilitation, because it reduces the sediment that reaches the water rather than only catching some of it.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by justifying rehabilitation with clear reasons linked to the creek, weighing the limitations of both practices and reaching a supported judgement.

sampleAnswers.answer: Progressive rehabilitation is more effective, because it stops erosion where the sediment starts. Sediment ponds are useful during mining, but they miss the finest clay particles.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by justifying a choice with relevant reasons, but the comparison of the two practices is limited.

sampleAnswers.answer: Sediment control is used at the mine, and rehabilitation is also used.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies two practices without a justified choice.

dotPoints.description: Assess the impact of mining on Aboriginal Cultural sites and Country in the Pilbara and one NSW location

prompts.question: OUTLINE two ways that mining can harm Aboriginal cultural sites and Country in the Pilbara, and the cultural significance that each harm affects.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A proposed iron ore expansion in the Pilbara would blast and excavate a gorge that Traditional Owners say contains rock shelters with artefacts and sites of cultural importance.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Outlines two specific ways mining can harm sites or Country, such as blasting rock shelters or disturbing waterways, each linked to its cultural significance
2 marks: Outlines one relevant way mining can harm a site or Country, without a link to its cultural significance
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about mining and Aboriginal cultural heritage
markerNotes: Name the specific site or Country affected and the way mining harms it.
Cultural significance is the link to the dot point: the harm matters because of what the site means to Traditional Owners.
commonStudentErrors: Naming a harm, such as pollution, without saying which cultural site or Country it affects.
Describing Aboriginal cultural heritage only as old objects, without its significance to Traditional Owners.

sampleAnswers.answer: Blasting and excavation can destroy Aboriginal cultural sites such as rock shelters in the Pilbara, removing physical evidence that forms part of the cultural heritage. Mining can also disturb Country itself, including waterways and landscapes linked to stories and ceremony, which breaks the connection that Traditional Owners hold with the land.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by outlining two harms and linking each to the cultural significance of the site or Country.

sampleAnswers.answer: Blasting can destroy rock shelters where artefacts are found.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by outlining one way mining harms a site, without linking it to its cultural significance.

sampleAnswers.answer: Mining can affect the land where Aboriginal people live.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Provides some relevant information, but does not name a specific way mining harms a cultural site.

prompts.question: ASSESS the impact of mining on Aboriginal cultural sites and Country, using the Juukan Gorge example in the Pilbara and the proposed valley mine in the scenario.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A coal mine extension in a New South Wales valley would clear a ridge with recorded scarred trees and a stone artefact scatter, and lower a creek that Traditional Owners use for ceremonies. In the Pilbara, a mining company blasted two rock shelters at Juukan Gorge in 2020, destroying sites that had been occupied for many thousands of years.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Assesses the impact at both locations in detail, weighing physical, cultural and water-related effects and the limits of each example, with a supported judgement about the scale of the impact
5 marks: Assesses the impact at both locations with relevant reasons, linking the effects to the cultural significance of the sites for Traditional Owners
4 marks: Assesses the impact at one location with relevant reasons, or describes both locations with some comparison
3 marks: Describes some impacts at the locations, with a basic link to Aboriginal cultural sites or Country
2 marks: Identifies one impact of mining on a cultural site, without assessing it
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about mining and Aboriginal cultural heritage
markerNotes: Assessment weighs the scale and permanence of the impact, such as whether destroyed sites can be recovered.
Use both locations from the scenario, and say what each example shows and what it cannot show.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the impact at each location without assessing how serious it is or whether it can be reversed.
Treating Aboriginal cultural sites as physical objects only, without their significance to Traditional Owners and Country.

sampleAnswers.answer: The Pilbara example shows the most severe and permanent form of impact: blasting destroyed rock shelters that had been occupied for many thousands of years, so the physical evidence cannot be recovered. The harm is also cultural, because these Aboriginal cultural sites are part of Country and of the knowledge Traditional Owners pass on. The New South Wales valley shows a different pattern. Clearing the ridge would remove scarred trees and an artefact scatter, and lowering the creek would affect ceremonies that depend on water in the landscape, so the mining impact extends beyond the mine footprint. However, both examples have limits. The Juukan Gorge case is a single event, and the New South Wales effects are predicted rather than measured, so they are uncertain. Overall, the impact is serious at both locations, and it is most serious where the destruction of sites cannot be reversed.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by assessing the impact at both locations, weighing physical and cultural effects, and stating the limits of each example before reaching a judgement.

sampleAnswers.answer: At Juukan Gorge, blasting destroyed rock shelters that Traditional Owners regard as part of Country, so the damage is permanent. In the New South Wales valley, clearing the ridge would damage recorded Aboriginal cultural sites, and lowering the creek would affect ceremonies. The impact is serious at both places, though the New South Wales effects are only predicted.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row by assessing the impact at both locations, with some comparison and a limited judgement.

sampleAnswers.answer: Blasting destroyed rock shelters at Juukan Gorge, which damaged an Aboriginal cultural site.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying one impact on a cultural site, without assessing it.

dotPoints.description: Compare the energy transformations involved in the generation of electric currents from turbines powered by coal, natural gas, wind and water

prompts.question: OUTLINE the energy transformations in a coal-fired power station, from the chemical energy stored in the coal to the electrical energy of the current produced.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A Year 11 class is preparing a poster that compares four power stations: a coal-fired station, a natural gas station, a wind farm and a hydro-electric dam. The first task is to set out the sequence of energy transformations for the coal-fired station.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Outlines the sequence of transformations in a coal-fired station, from chemical energy in the coal to thermal, kinetic and electrical energy, and explains the role of the turbine and generator
3 marks: Outlines the main sequence of transformations, naming most stages and the role of the turbine
2 marks: Identifies some energy forms or stages in the process, without a clear sequence
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about power generation
markerNotes: Set out the stages in order and name the form of energy at each one.
The generator is what produces the electric current; the turbine supplies the kinetic energy that drives it.
commonStudentErrors: Saying the turbine makes electricity directly from coal, skipping the heating and steam stages.
Describing energy as being created at a stage, rather than transformed from one form into another.

sampleAnswers.answer: In a coal-fired station, the chemical energy stored in coal is transformed into thermal energy when the coal is burned, so the first of the energy transformations is chemical to thermal. The heat boils water into steam, and the steam transfers its kinetic energy to a turbine, which spins. The turbine drives a generator, which transforms kinetic energy into the electrical energy of an electric current. Some energy is lost as waste heat along the way, so the output is less than the energy stored in the coal.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row by setting out the sequence from chemical to thermal, kinetic and electrical energy, with the roles of the turbine and generator explained.

sampleAnswers.answer: Coal is burned to make heat and steam. The steam turns a turbine that makes electricity.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying some stages, but the sequence is not clear and the generator's role is missing.

sampleAnswers.answer: Coal is burned to make electricity.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Provides some relevant information about coal in power generation, without setting out the stages.

prompts.question: ANALYSE the energy transformations behind the electric current from turbines powered by coal, natural gas, wind and water, identifying the stages the four methods share and where they differ.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A regional council is comparing four electricity options for a new town: a coal-fired station, a natural gas station, a wind farm on an open ridge and a hydro-electric dam on a river. The council wants to understand why each source produces electricity in the way it does.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses the energy transformations for all four methods, separating the shared stages from the differences and explaining the energy form at each stage
5 marks: Analyses the transformations for most methods, identifying shared stages and at least two differences with relevant reasons
4 marks: Analyses the transformations for some methods, identifying a shared stage and a difference with a limited explanation
3 marks: Describes the energy sources and some stages, with a basic comparison of the methods
2 marks: Identifies one stage or one energy source, without analysing the transformations
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about electricity generation
markerNotes: Analysis separates the shared stages, the turbine and generator, from the first transformation, which differs by energy source.
Name the energy form at each stage, such as chemical, thermal, kinetic, gravitational and electrical.
commonStudentErrors: Listing the energy source of each method without analysing the transformations between stages.
Saying wind or water turbines need a boiler or steam stage, which they do not.

sampleAnswers.answer: All four methods end with a turbine driving a generator, so each produces an electric current by transforming kinetic energy into electrical energy. The energy transformations differ in the energy they start with and in the stages before the turbine. Coal and natural gas both store chemical energy, which is released as thermal energy when burned. In a steam station the heat boils water and the steam turns the turbine, while a gas turbine can be driven directly by hot combustion gases. Wind has no heating stage: the kinetic energy of moving air turns the blades, which turn the generator. Water starts with gravitational potential energy, which becomes kinetic energy as it falls to the turbine. The shared stages are the turbine and generator, and the first transformation, from chemical, kinetic or gravitational energy, is what distinguishes the four.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by analysing all four transformations, separating the shared stages from the differences and naming the energy form at each stage.

sampleAnswers.answer: All four methods use a turbine to drive a generator, which produces the electric current. Coal and gas start with chemical energy that is released as heat, while wind and water start with kinetic or gravitational energy. Coal and gas therefore have an extra heating stage that wind and water do not.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row by identifying a shared stage and a difference, with a limited explanation of the transformations.

sampleAnswers.answer: The turbine and generator are used by all four methods, but the energy source differs.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies a shared stage and a difference, without analysing the transformations.

dotPoints.description: Conduct a practical investigation to generate an electric current using a turbine

prompts.question: DESCRIBE how students should set up a practical investigation to generate an electric current with a small turbine, naming the equipment and how the voltage is recorded.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: Students fix a small plastic turbine to the shaft of a hand-cranked generator. Water from a tank at a fixed height is poured onto the blades, and a voltmeter is connected across the generator's terminals.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Describes a complete set-up, naming the turbine, generator, water supply and voltmeter in order, and how the voltage is recorded and repeated
3 marks: Describes most of the set-up in order, naming the main equipment and how the voltage is read
2 marks: Identifies some of the equipment for the set-up, without a clear sequence
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about generating electricity with a turbine
markerNotes: Describe the set-up in the order it is built, so the reader can follow how the turbine drives the generator.
A repeated trial with the same water flow is what makes the readings reliable.
commonStudentErrors: Listing the equipment without saying how it is connected or in what order.
Recording only one voltage reading, without repeating the trial to check consistency.

sampleAnswers.answer: This practical investigation begins as students mount the plastic turbine on the shaft of the hand-cranked generator so that the blades turn freely in the water. The voltmeter is connected across the generator's terminals to record the voltage of the electric current produced. They pour water from the fixed-height tank onto the blades at a steady water flow and read the voltmeter at set intervals. Each trial is repeated with the same water flow to check that the readings are consistent before the results are compared.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row by describing the complete set-up in order, with the voltage recorded and each trial repeated.

sampleAnswers.answer: Students use a turbine, a generator and a voltmeter, and they pour water onto the blades.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying some of the equipment, without a clear sequence or a method for recording the voltage.

sampleAnswers.answer: A turbine is turned by water to make electricity.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Provides some relevant information about generating electricity with a turbine, but no set-up is described.

prompts.question: ASSESS the validity of the students' conclusion, identifying the variables that were not controlled and suggesting one improvement to the practical investigation.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: Students test a small turbine with a hair dryer blowing air onto the blades in one trial, and a tap running water onto the blades in another. They record the voltage each time and conclude that wind is a better energy source than water for generating electricity.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Assesses the validity of the conclusion in detail, identifying several uncontrolled variables and their effect on the electric current, and suggesting a practical improvement with a supported judgement
5 marks: Assesses the conclusion with relevant reasons, identifying at least two uncontrolled variables and linking them to the reliability of the results
4 marks: Assesses the conclusion by identifying some reasons it is valid or invalid and at least one uncontrolled variable, with a limited judgement
3 marks: Identifies some features of the investigation, with a basic link to the validity of the conclusion
2 marks: Identifies one feature of the investigation, without assessing its validity
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the investigation
markerNotes: Validity depends on changing only the variable being tested, so identify the other factors that changed between trials.
An improvement must address a named uncontrolled variable and say how to hold it constant.
commonStudentErrors: Accepting the conclusion without noticing that two energy sources were tested with different inputs.
Listing the turbine as an uncontrolled variable when it was kept the same in both trials.

sampleAnswers.answer: The conclusion is not valid because the investigation changes more than one variable. The hair dryer and the tap differ in the force, speed and volume of the flow reaching the blades, so the differences in voltage may come from the flow rather than from the energy source. The blades, their angle and the distance from the outlet to the blades were probably not identical, and the generator's contact with the shaft may also have varied between trials. These uncontrolled variables mean the practical investigation cannot show that wind gives more electric current than water. One improvement is to measure the flow speed for each energy source and keep it the same across all trials, so that only the energy source differs. The same turbine should be used in every trial and each trial should be repeated, so the validity of the voltage readings can be checked. Only the energy source should change between trials, while everything else is controlled.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by identifying several uncontrolled variables, linking them to the electric current and suggesting a practical improvement with a supported judgement.

sampleAnswers.answer: The conclusion is not valid, because the hair dryer and the tap produce different flows and the test changes more than the energy source. The blades and the distance to the outlet may also have differed between trials.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by identifying why the conclusion is invalid and two uncontrolled variables, but no improvement is suggested.

sampleAnswers.answer: The students used a hair dryer and a tap, which are different.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies one feature of the investigation, without assessing its validity.

dotPoints.description: Conduct a practical investigation to gather quantitative data on a factor affecting the power output of a photovoltaic cell

prompts.question: DESCRIBE how students should measure the power output of a small photovoltaic cell at different light intensities, naming the equipment and the variables kept constant.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: Students place a small photovoltaic cell under a lamp at set distances to vary the light intensity. They connect the cell to a voltmeter and an ammeter to measure its output at each distance.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Describes a complete method, naming the equipment, the independent and dependent variables, the variables kept constant and how the quantitative data are recorded
3 marks: Describes most of the method, naming the main equipment and variables and how the data are recorded
2 marks: Identifies some equipment or variables for the investigation, without a full method
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about measuring a photovoltaic cell
markerNotes: Name the independent and dependent variables, and the variables held constant, rather than only the equipment.
Say how each reading is recorded, such as in a table of current and voltage at each distance.
commonStudentErrors: Changing the light intensity and the cell's temperature together, so the output cannot be linked to one factor.
Recording only one reading at each light intensity, without repeating the measurement.

sampleAnswers.answer: This practical investigation measures the power output of the photovoltaic cell by placing it under the lamp at set distances, which sets the light intensity. The voltmeter and ammeter are connected to the cell's terminals to record the voltage and current at each distance, moving the lamp in equal steps to gather quantitative data. The independent variable is the distance from the lamp and the dependent variable is the output, and the other variables kept constant are the cell's angle, its temperature and the lamp's power. Each distance is repeated and the readings are recorded in a table.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row by describing a complete method with the variables named, the constant variables held and the data recorded.

sampleAnswers.answer: Students use a photovoltaic cell, a lamp, a voltmeter and an ammeter to measure the output at different distances.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying the equipment and the variable changed, without a full method.

sampleAnswers.answer: A photovoltaic cell turns light into electricity.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Provides some relevant information about photovoltaic cells, but does not describe a method.

prompts.question: ASSESS how well this investigation design controls for other factors that affect photovoltaic output, and suggest one improvement that would make the quantitative data more valid.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: Students measure the output of one cell at five lamp distances in a classroom, with the lamp at a fixed angle. During the lesson the room temperature rises, a student's hand sometimes shades the cell, and the lamp's bulb heats the cell's surface.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Assesses the design in detail, identifying several uncontrolled factors and their effect on the photovoltaic output, and suggests an improvement with a supported judgement on the validity of the data
5 marks: Assesses the design with relevant reasons, identifying at least two uncontrolled factors and linking them to the quantitative data
4 marks: Assesses the design by identifying one or two uncontrolled factors and their effect on validity, with a limited judgement
3 marks: Identifies some features of the design and some factors it does not control, with a basic link to the data
2 marks: Identifies one feature of the design, without assessing how well it controls other factors
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the investigation
markerNotes: Name each uncontrolled factor and say how it changes the output, rather than listing general problems.
An improvement must hold a named factor constant, such as by shielding the cell from the lamp's heat.
commonStudentErrors: Saying the design is valid because the readings were repeated, without checking the other factors.
Suggesting an improvement that changes the variable being tested, such as adding lamps at different angles.

sampleAnswers.answer: The design controls the lamp's angle, but it does not control several variables that affect photovoltaic output. Temperature is the most serious: a rising room temperature and the heat from the lamp's bulb both reduce the efficiency of the cell, so the output falls for reasons other than light intensity. A student's hand also casts shadows that change the light reaching the cell unevenly. Measuring at five distances in one lesson means the readings are taken at different times and temperatures. Overall, the design gives a fair test of distance only if temperature and shading are held constant, and the validity of the quantitative data is limited without that control. One improvement is to shield the cell from the lamp's heat, fix a frame to prevent shading, and take each reading after the cell reaches a steady temperature.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by identifying several uncontrolled variables, explaining their effect on output and suggesting an improvement with a supported judgement on validity.

sampleAnswers.answer: The design does not control temperature, because the room warms and the lamp heats the cell, so the output falls for reasons other than distance. A student's shadow can also change the light, which reduces the validity of the data.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row by identifying two uncontrolled factors and their effect on validity, with no improvement suggested.

sampleAnswers.answer: The lamp is kept at a fixed angle, so the design controls one thing.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies one feature of the design, without assessing how well it controls other factors.

dotPoints.description: Relate the locations of existing Australian power generation from coal, natural gas, wind farm, solar farm and hydro-electric to environmental, topographic and population data

prompts.question: CLASSIFY each of the five power sources in the scenario by the kind of location it needs, using the environmental, topographic and population data shown on the map.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A map shows the locations of a coal-fired station, a natural gas plant, a wind farm, a solar farm and a hydro-electric station in one region. Overlays show land elevation, rainfall, sunshine hours and population density across the same region.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Classifies each power source by the location it needs, linking at least three sources to environmental, topographic or population data
2 marks: Classifies some sources by location, with a basic link to one type of data
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about power generation locations
markerNotes: Classify each source by the location it needs, and name the data type that shows it.
Population can be a constraint as well as a benefit, such as distance from towns for noise or for transmission.
commonStudentErrors: Listing the power sources without stating the kind of location each one needs.
Saying coal stations need sunshine or rainfall, which are not the controlling factors for them.

sampleAnswers.answer: Coal and natural gas stations are forms of power generation that need fuel supply and cooling water, so they are classified by environmental and population data, usually away from dense housing. A hydro-electric station needs a steep valley, which topographic data reveal, and a reliable rainfall catchment. A wind farm and a solar farm need open, exposed land with strong winds or high sunshine, which environmental data show.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by classifying each source by the location it needs and linking several sources to environmental, topographic or population data.

sampleAnswers.answer: Hydro-electric stations need steep valleys and rainfall, and wind farms need open land.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by classifying some sources by location, with a basic link to topographic and environmental data.

sampleAnswers.answer: Solar farms need sunshine to produce power.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Provides some relevant information about one power source, without classifying the locations of the sources.

prompts.question: ANALYSE how the sites of the coal-fired station and the wind farm relate to the topographic, environmental and population data shown on the map in the scenario.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A coal-fired station sits on flat land beside a major river and a coalfield, about 60 kilometres from a large city. A wind farm is placed on an exposed coastal ridge, away from towns, where the wind is strongest and the population density is very low.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses how each site relates to topographic, environmental and population data, explaining the reason for each site and the constraints that the data reveal
5 marks: Analyses both sites with relevant reasons linked to at least two types of data
4 marks: Analyses one or both sites with some relevant reasons, linking them to one or two types of data
3 marks: Describes features of the sites, with a basic link to the data
2 marks: Identifies one feature of the sites, without linking it to the data
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the sites
markerNotes: Explain the site choice as a response to a resource, such as the coalfield or the wind, rather than only describing the site.
Population data can show a constraint on a site, such as noise or land use, as well as a benefit.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the features of each site without saying which data type shows why it was chosen.
Assuming wind farms need flat land, when an exposed ridge is often a stronger site.

sampleAnswers.answer: Power generation at the coal-fired station relates first to topographic data. Its flat land allows a large plant, and its cooling water is drawn from the river, while its position beside the coalfield reduces the cost of moving coal. Population data also matter: the station is about 60 kilometres from the city, close enough to supply demand but far enough to limit air and noise impacts on residents. The wind farm site relates to a different feature. An exposed coastal ridge increases wind speed, so the turbines produce more power, and its height and exposure are its strengths. Its low population density reduces conflict over noise and visual impact, while environmental data would show whether the ridge contains habitat that the turbines could affect. Together, the two sites show that each is placed to suit the resource it uses and the constraints of its surroundings.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by analysing how each site relates to topographic, environmental and population data and explaining the constraints each site must meet.

sampleAnswers.answer: The coal-fired station sits on flat land beside a river and a coalfield, which suits its cooling and fuel needs. The wind farm is on an exposed ridge, where strong winds suit it, and its low population density limits the impact on residents. Both sites relate to topographic and population data, though environmental data are used less.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row by analysing both sites with some relevant reasons, linked to topographic and population data.

sampleAnswers.answer: The coal station is near a river and the wind farm is on a ridge.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies one feature of each site, without linking it to the data.

dotPoints.description: Conduct a secondary-source investigation to evaluate the capacity of potential future renewable power generation sites using sunlight, wind, rainfall, topographic and population data

prompts.question: EXPLAIN why sunlight, wind and rainfall data are each used when assessing a potential renewable power generation site.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A planning team is reviewing possible sites for future renewable power generation using a secondary-source study. The team has a sunshine map, wind speed records, rainfall totals, a topographic map of ridges and valleys, and census data on population within 50 kilometres of each site.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Explains the purpose of each data type for the energy resource it measures, linking sunlight to solar output, wind to turbine output and rainfall to hydro-electric supply
2 marks: Explains the purpose of one or two data types, without linking them to a specific power source
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the data used to assess renewable sites
markerNotes: Link each data type to the resource it measures and the power source that resource determines.
Explain why the data matter, not only what they measure.
commonStudentErrors: Listing the data types without explaining what each shows about the energy resource.
Explaining wind data as showing how much sunlight reaches a site.

sampleAnswers.answer: Sunlight data show how much solar energy reaches the site, which sets the output of a solar farm. Wind data show the speed and steadiness of the air, which determines how much power a wind farm produces. Rainfall data show the water supply that a hydro-electric station depends on. Topographic and population data then show whether each renewable power generation site is practical.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining the purpose of each data type and linking it to the power source it determines.

sampleAnswers.answer: Wind data are used because wind is needed to assess a site.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by explaining the purpose of one data type in general terms, without linking it to a power source.

sampleAnswers.answer: The team uses data to decide which site is best.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Provides some relevant information about assessing sites, without explaining any data type.

prompts.question: ASSESS the capacity of Site A and Site B for a future renewable power station, using the sunlight, wind, rainfall, topographic and population data from the secondary-source study in the scenario.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A secondary-source study compares two sites. Site A is an exposed inland plateau with strong, steady winds, high sunshine, low rainfall, flat terrain and few residents. Site B is a coastal hill with moderate wind and sunshine, heavy rain, steep slopes and a town of 20,000 people within 10 kilometres.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Assesses the capacity of both sites in detail, weighing each data type against the resource it measures and reaching a supported judgement on which site has the greater capacity for each power source
5 marks: Assesses both sites with relevant reasons, using at least three data types and linking them to capacity
4 marks: Assesses one or both sites with some strengths and at least one limitation, with a limited judgement
3 marks: Describes features of the sites, with a basic link to capacity for renewable power generation
2 marks: Identifies one feature of one site, without assessing capacity
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the data used to assess sites
markerNotes: Judge capacity separately for each power source before reaching an overall view.
Population data can limit a site as well as support it, such as through land use or objections from residents.
commonStudentErrors: Comparing the sites on one data type only, such as wind, without judging overall capacity.
Saying Site B is unsuitable because it has rain, without linking heavy rain to hydro-electric capacity.

sampleAnswers.answer: Site A has the stronger capacity for wind and solar power, because its sunlight and wind data are the strongest of the two sites. Its strong, steady winds and high sunshine give high output, and its flat terrain, shown by the topographic data, allows turbines and panels to be placed efficiently. Its low rainfall means there is little water for hydro-electric generation, so that option is not viable there. The few residents mean the population data show low conflict over land use and noise. Site B's capacity is different. Heavy rain would support a hydro-electric scheme if the steep slopes can hold a reservoir, and its moderate wind and sunshine would give less output than Site A for wind or solar. The town 10 kilometres away offers a nearby market for power, but also a source of objections. Overall, Site A has the greater capacity for renewable power generation, while Site B's value lies in its hydro-electric potential rather than in wind or solar.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by weighing the data for each power source and reaching a supported judgement on which site has the greater capacity.

sampleAnswers.answer: Site A's strong wind and high sunshine give it good capacity for wind and solar power, and its flat terrain makes construction easier. Site B's heavy rain suits hydro-electric power, but its steep slopes limit the other options.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by assessing both sites with a strength and a limitation for each, though the judgement stays limited.

sampleAnswers.answer: Site A has strong winds, so it is better for wind power.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies one feature of one site, without assessing the capacity of both sites.

dotPoints.description: Explain the role of consultation with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples when considering potential power generation sites

prompts.question: Using the scenario, OUTLINE two reasons why the company should consult the Local Aboriginal Land Council before it chooses the site.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A company plans to build a large solar farm on grazing land beside a river in western New South Wales. A Local Aboriginal Land Council has asked to be consulted before any site is chosen. It says the area contains places of cultural significance and that Aboriginal people hold long-term knowledge of the land and the river.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Outlines two distinct reasons for consultation, each linked to the scenario
2 marks: Outlines one reason for consultation linked to the scenario, or two reasons with limited links to the scenario
1 mark: Identifies a relevant idea about consultation
keywords: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples
markerNotes: Each reason should say what consultation achieves for this site, such as protecting places or using knowledge, rather than only saying that consultation should happen.
Link each reason to the scenario's cultural places or the river knowledge so the answer shows the site is understood.
commonStudentErrors: Stating that consultation is a good idea without saying what it achieves for the site.
Giving two versions of the same reason, such as 'it is respectful' and 'it shows respect', instead of two distinct reasons.

sampleAnswers.answer: Consultation with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples through the Local Aboriginal Land Council lets the company find where places of cultural significance are, so the solar farm can avoid damaging them. Their long-term knowledge of the land and river can also help the company choose power generation sites that are practical and suit the community.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by outlining two distinct reasons, protecting cultural places and using long-term knowledge, each linked to the scenario.

sampleAnswers.answer: Consulting the Local Aboriginal Land Council lets the company avoid damaging places of cultural significance during construction.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Outlines one reason linked to the scenario and gives no second reason, so it meets the 2-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The company should talk to the local community before it builds anything.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies a relevant idea about consultation but does not outline a reason linked to the scenario.

prompts.question: The project manager argues that consulting Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples only slows the project and adds cost. Using the scenario, ASSESS this claim.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A project manager tells the board that talks with the Local Aboriginal Land Council about the proposed solar farm will slow the approvals process and add cost. The Land Council wants to share its knowledge of the land and river and to identify places of cultural significance before any site is confirmed.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Makes a sustained, well-reasoned judgement of the claim, weighing the time and cost of consultation against its benefits for site selection and project outcomes
5 marks: Assesses the claim with relevant reasons on both sides, linked to the scenario
4 marks: Makes a judgement on the claim, supported by some relevant reasons linked to the scenario
3 marks: Describes a role of consultation that has some relevance to the claim
2 marks: Identifies a cost or benefit of consultation with limited link to the claim
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
keywords: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples
markerNotes: Make a clear judgement on the claim first, then weigh the time and cost of consultation against what it gives the project, rather than listing both sides without a conclusion.
Use the scenario's detail, such as places of cultural significance and the Land Council's knowledge of the river, to support the judgement.
commonStudentErrors: Describing consultation without judging the project manager's claim.
Treating consultation only as a cost, without considering how it can change site selection or reduce later disputes.

sampleAnswers.answer: The claim is partly correct but overstated. Consultation can add time and cost, because the company must arrange meetings, gather information and possibly change the layout of the power generation design. However, talking with the Local Aboriginal Land Council early allows the company to identify places of cultural significance before site selection is complete, so the layout can avoid them and the project does not face costly disputes or delays later. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples also hold knowledge of the land and river that can improve the design and reduce environmental risk. Ignoring this knowledge risks rework, lost trust and approval delays, which are often more costly than the consultation itself. On balance, consultation is a short-term cost that is more likely to reduce long-term delay and cost, so the claim is not well supported.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Makes a sustained judgement that weighs the cost of consultation against its benefits for site selection and risk, and supports the conclusion with the scenario.

sampleAnswers.answer: Consultation adds time and cost, so the claim has some truth. However, talking to the Land Council can also help the company find places of cultural significance before the site is chosen, which may avoid later problems. The claim ignores these benefits.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Makes a judgement on the claim with some relevant reasons linked to the scenario, but does not weigh the points as fully as the top row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Consultation takes time, which could delay the solar farm.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies a cost of consultation with limited link to the claim and no judgement, so it meets the 2-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Assess the need for energy storage associated with solar and wind power generation

prompts.question: Using the scenario, EXPLAIN why the solar farm and the wind farm together still need energy storage to supply the town.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A town in western New South Wales plans to connect a solar farm and a wind farm to its local electricity supply. Residents use most of their electricity in the evening, after dark. The solar farm produces power only while the sun shines, and the wind farm produces little power on calm days.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Explains that solar and wind output does not match evening demand, and that storage is needed to hold energy for later use, with both points linked to the scenario
2 marks: Explains that solar or wind output varies, with a link to the scenario
1 mark: Identifies a relevant feature of solar or wind power
markerNotes: A strong answer names the mismatch in timing, such as solar stopping at dusk, and then explains what storage does about it.
Use the word intermittent or an equivalent to show that the output of both sources changes with weather.
commonStudentErrors: Stating that solar and wind are renewable without explaining why the town still needs storage.
Saying that storage makes electricity cheaper, which is not what the question asks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Solar power and wind power are intermittent, because the panels produce electricity only while the sun shines and the wind farm depends on wind speed. In the scenario, electricity demand is highest in the evening, after dark, when the solar farm is not producing. Energy storage, such as batteries, can hold surplus daytime power and release it when demand is high.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains the mismatch between output and evening demand and why storage is needed to hold energy, with both points linked to the scenario.

sampleAnswers.answer: The solar farm produces power only while the sun shines, so it cannot supply the evening electricity demand in the scenario.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains that solar output varies, with a link to the scenario, but does not explain the need for storage.

sampleAnswers.answer: Solar and wind power are weather dependent.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies a relevant feature of solar and wind power without explaining why storage is needed.

prompts.question: Using the scenario, RECOMMEND one energy storage option for the town's solar and wind farms and give reasons for your choice.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A regional council must choose one storage option for the town's new solar and wind farms. The first option is a large battery system built beside the solar farm. The second is a pumped hydro scheme, which would need two water storages at different heights and a large construction project. The council has limited funds and wants a reliable supply overnight.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Recommends one storage option with sustained reasoning that weighs reliability, cost and construction against the scenario's needs
5 marks: Recommends one storage option with clear reasons linked to the scenario, with some weighing of its limitations
4 marks: Recommends a storage option with relevant reasons linked to the scenario
3 marks: Describes a feature of one storage option that relates to the scenario
2 marks: Identifies a storage option without linking it to the scenario
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: State the recommendation clearly at the start, then give reasons that compare the options against what the scenario asks for, such as overnight reliability and limited funds.
Acknowledge at least one limitation of the chosen option, which shows that the judgement is balanced.
commonStudentErrors: Recommending an option with general reasons, such as 'batteries are good', instead of linking them to the scenario.
Describing both options without making a recommendation.

sampleAnswers.answer: I recommend a large battery system built beside the solar farm. Batteries can store daytime solar power and release it overnight, which gives a reliable supply for the town when the solar farm and wind farm are not producing. They can also respond quickly to changes in demand, so they can balance the output from the wind power when wind speeds drop. A battery system needs less construction than pumped hydro, which would require two water storages at different heights, so it suits a council with limited funds. Batteries can also be expanded in stages as the town's needs grow, which spreads the cost over time. Batteries do have limits: they store energy for shorter periods than pumped hydro and lose capacity over time, so the council should plan for replacement. Even so, this battery system is the most practical and affordable energy storage for the town.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Recommends a battery system with sustained reasoning that weighs reliability and cost against the scenario, and acknowledges its limits.

sampleAnswers.answer: I recommend batteries beside the solar farm, because they can store daytime electricity for use in the evening. Batteries also cost less to build than a pumped hydro scheme, which suits the council's limited funds.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Recommends an option with two relevant reasons linked to the scenario, but does not weigh limitations, so it meets the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The council should choose batteries because they are a type of energy storage.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies an option without linking the reasons to the scenario's needs, so it meets the 2-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Conduct a secondary-source investigation to compare the main uses of energy in Australian society

prompts.question: Using the scenario, CLASSIFY each of the four main uses of energy as household, industrial, transport or services use.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A Year 11 student summarises a secondary source, a state energy report, for a regional city. The report lists four main uses of energy: driving cars, trucks and buses; heating, cooling and running appliances in homes; operating factories and mines; and running schools, hospitals and offices.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Classifies all four uses correctly and gives a reason for each from the scenario
3 marks: Classifies three uses correctly, with a reason for each
2 marks: Classifies two uses correctly
1 mark: Classifies one use correctly
markerNotes: Classify each use by the sector it serves, using the scenario's wording, rather than by the type of fuel.
Give a short reason for each classification so the answer shows why the use belongs in that sector.
commonStudentErrors: Classifying the use by fuel, such as calling driving an oil use, instead of by the sector it serves.
Placing schools, hospitals and offices under household use because they are buildings.

sampleAnswers.answer: Driving cars, trucks and buses is transport energy use, because it moves people and freight. Heating, cooling and running appliances in homes is household energy use, because it supports daily life in houses. Operating factories and mines is industrial energy use, because it powers production and extraction. Running schools, hospitals and offices is services energy use, because it supports public and commercial buildings that provide services to the community. Each use is grouped by the sector that consumes the energy, not by the fuel used, so the classification depends on who is using the energy.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Classifies all four uses correctly, with a reason for each drawn from the scenario, so it meets the top row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Driving cars and buses is transport use, and operating factories and mines is industrial use.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Classifies two uses correctly without reasons, so it meets the 2-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Heating homes is a household use.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Classifies one use correctly, so it meets the 1-mark row.

prompts.question: Using the scenario, DISCUSS how the main uses of energy in Australian society affect the choice between fossil fuels and renewable electricity.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: The same state energy report notes that transport relies mostly on liquid fuels, while households and services rely mainly on electricity and gas. It also notes that factories and mines use large amounts of energy for heating and processing, and that the state government wants to shift more of its electricity supply to renewable sources.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Discusses how each main use of energy shapes the choice between fossil fuels and renewable electricity, with sustained reasoning and clear links to the scenario
5 marks: Discusses at least two uses and how they affect the choice of energy source, with relevant reasoning from the scenario
4 marks: Discusses one or two uses and how they relate to the choice of energy source
3 marks: Describes a use of energy and an energy source linked to it
2 marks: Identifies a use of energy or an energy source with limited link
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Discuss each main use separately, because transport, households and industry rely on different energy sources and have different needs for reliability.
Support each point with a detail from the scenario, such as liquid fuels for transport or electricity for homes.
commonStudentErrors: Listing the energy uses without discussing how they affect the choice between fossil fuels and renewable electricity.
Claiming that all uses can switch to renewable electricity immediately, without considering reliability or cost.

sampleAnswers.answer: The main uses of energy shape how easily the state can move from fossil fuels to renewable electricity. Transport relies mostly on liquid fuels, which are difficult to replace directly for cars, trucks and buses, so transport keeps much of its demand for fossil fuels in the short term, although electric vehicles are growing in use. Household and services use is mainly electricity and gas, so a shift to renewable electricity can cut emissions quickly for heating, cooling and appliances. Industrial use in factories and mines needs high-temperature heat and large, continuous supplies, which makes the choice harder because renewable electricity must be reliable enough for processing. Energy policy must therefore treat each use separately, with renewable electricity leading in households and services while industry and transport change more slowly. Without that balance, a plan that targets only one sector would leave the others dependent on fossil fuels.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Discusses how each major use shapes the choice of energy source, with sustained reasoning and clear links to the scenario.

sampleAnswers.answer: Transport relies on liquid fuels, so cars and trucks still need fossil fuels. Households and services use electricity, so renewable electricity can replace more of their energy use more easily.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Discusses two uses and how they relate to the choice of energy source, with some reasoning, so it meets the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Transport uses liquid fuels, which are fossil fuels.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies a use and an energy source with limited link to the choice, so it meets the 2-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Justify the use of renewable and non-renewable sources to generate electricity

prompts.question: Using the scenario, DESCRIBE one advantage and one disadvantage of using coal to generate the town's electricity.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A town council is considering whether to keep buying electricity from a coal-fired power station, which burns coal from a nearby mine. Coal is a non-renewable resource. Residents want a supply that is reliable and that produces low carbon dioxide emissions.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes an advantage and a disadvantage of coal, each linked to the scenario
2 marks: Describes an advantage or a disadvantage of coal with some link to the scenario
1 mark: Identifies a relevant feature of coal or its use
markerNotes: Name both an advantage and a disadvantage, and link each one to the reliability or emissions concerns in the scenario.
Describe why the feature matters rather than just naming it, such as why a non-renewable fuel will eventually run out.
commonStudentErrors: Describing only the advantage of coal, such as that it is cheap, without a disadvantage.
Calling coal renewable, or describing it as clean because it produces electricity reliably.

sampleAnswers.answer: An advantage of coal-fired electricity generation is that the power station runs continuously, so it provides a reliable supply of electricity regardless of the weather. A disadvantage is that burning coal releases carbon dioxide, which adds to emissions and to climate change. Coal is also a non-renewable resource, so the mine will eventually run out.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes an advantage and a disadvantage of coal, each linked to the scenario's reliability and emissions concerns.

sampleAnswers.answer: Coal can run continuously, so it gives a reliable supply in the town.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes an advantage of coal with some link to the scenario but no disadvantage, so it meets the 2-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Coal is a non-renewable resource that is burned to produce electricity.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies a relevant feature of coal without describing an advantage or disadvantage.

prompts.question: Using the scenario, JUSTIFY which generator the council should choose for the town's electricity supply, based on reliability, emissions and fuel supply.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A regional town has been offered two new generators. The first is a coal-fired power station that would run continuously on coal from a nearby mine, a non-renewable fuel. The second is a wind farm on the ridgeline above the town, which produces power only when the wind blows. The council must choose one generator and must consider reliability, carbon dioxide emissions and fuel supply.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Justifies a clear choice of generator with sustained reasoning that weighs reliability, emissions and fuel supply against each other
5 marks: Justifies a choice with clear reasons linked to the scenario, with some weighing of the alternative
4 marks: Justifies a choice with relevant reasons linked to the scenario
3 marks: Describes a feature of one generator that relates to the criteria
2 marks: Identifies a criterion or generator with limited link to the choice
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: State the choice clearly, then argue why it is better on the criteria in the scenario rather than only describing each generator.
Weigh reliability against emissions and fuel supply, because the strongest answers recognise the trade-off.
commonStudentErrors: Stating a choice without giving reasons based on the three criteria.
Saying that wind is good because it is renewable, without mentioning that it only produces power when the wind blows.

sampleAnswers.answer: The council should choose the wind farm, because it best balances the three criteria for a town's electricity supply, although it needs to be paired with storage or backup. The coal-fired station is reliable because it runs continuously, but its fuel supply is non-renewable and depends on a mine with limited reserves. Burning coal also releases carbon dioxide, which increases the town's emissions. The wind farm uses a renewable resource with no fuel supply to run out and produces no carbon dioxide while operating. Coal supplies from a nearby mine can also be disrupted by mine closures or price changes, which adds risk to the fuel supply. Its main weakness is reliability, since it produces power only when the wind blows, so the council should not rely on it alone. On balance, the renewable wind farm is the better long-term choice, provided the council plans for periods of calm weather.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Justifies the wind farm with sustained reasoning that weighs reliability against emissions and fuel supply, and acknowledges the trade-off.

sampleAnswers.answer: The council should choose the wind farm, because wind power is renewable and produces no carbon dioxide while it runs. However, it only produces power when the wind blows, so the town may need backup power.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Justifies a choice with relevant reasons linked to the scenario, but gives less weighing of the alternative, so it meets the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Reliability matters, and the coal-fired station runs all the time.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies a criterion and one generator with limited link to a choice, so it meets the 2-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Relate supply and demand to the need for a mix of sources to supply energy

prompts.question: Using the scenario, PREDICT what would happen to the town's electricity supply on the still, hot afternoon, and give a reason for your prediction.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A town relies on a single wind farm for most of its electricity. On a still, hot afternoon, the wind farm produces little power while many households switch on air-conditioners, so the town's electricity demand is at its highest. The only other generator in the town is a small gas unit that is not running at that time.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Predicts that supply falls short of demand, and explains that wind output depends on wind speed, linked to the scenario
2 marks: Predicts a shortfall in supply with limited explanation
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about wind power or electricity demand
markerNotes: Predict the direction of the change clearly, such as a shortfall, before giving the reason.
Link the reason to the specific conditions in the scenario, such as the still air and the peak demand from air-conditioners.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the scenario without predicting what happens to supply.
Saying the town would have problems with electricity without naming the shortfall or its cause.

sampleAnswers.answer: The town's electricity supply would fall short of the demand, because wind power depends on wind speed and the wind farm produces little on a still afternoon. At the same time, air-conditioners push electricity demand to its highest, so the shortfall is likely to be large unless the gas unit starts.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Predicts a shortfall between supply and demand and explains the link to wind speed, linked to the scenario.

sampleAnswers.answer: The supply would fall short of the demand, since the wind farm is not producing much.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Predicts a shortfall with limited explanation, so it meets the 2-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Air-conditioners increase electricity demand in the afternoon.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Provides relevant information about electricity demand without predicting the effect on supply.

prompts.question: Using the scenario, DISCUSS how the pattern of supply and demand in the town supports the need for a mix of sources.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A town's electricity comes from three sources: a solar farm, a wind farm and a gas-fired generator. Demand is highest in the evening and on hot days, when air-conditioning is used, and lowest overnight. The solar farm produces power only during daylight hours, the wind farm varies with wind speed, and the gas-fired generator can be started quickly to add power when supply falls short.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Discusses how the timing and variability of supply and demand together justify a mix of sources, with sustained reasoning linked to all three sources in the scenario
5 marks: Discusses how supply and demand patterns support a mix of sources, with clear links to the scenario
4 marks: Discusses the need for more than one source, with some links to the scenario
3 marks: Describes a mismatch between supply and demand linked to one source
2 marks: Identifies a source of supply or a pattern of demand with limited link
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Explain why a mix works, such as one source covering a gap in another, so the answer discusses the need rather than only stating it.
Use the timing of solar power and the variability of wind power from the scenario to show where the mismatch occurs.
commonStudentErrors: Stating that a mix of sources is good for the environment without discussing supply and demand.
Saying that solar and wind always supply enough power, which ignores their variability.

sampleAnswers.answer: Supply and demand in this town do not match at the same times, which is why a mix of sources is needed. Peak demand comes in the evening and on hot days, when air-conditioning is used, but solar power stops at dusk, so the solar farm cannot meet the evening demand. Wind power varies with wind speed, so the wind farm may produce little at the moments when demand is highest. Relying on one source would leave gaps in supply. The gas-fired generator fills these gaps because it can start quickly, but it is a fossil fuel source with emissions. A mix of sources, with solar power covering the daytime, wind adding output when it blows and the gas generator covering shortfalls, lets the town match supply to demand across the day while reducing reliance on gas. The pattern therefore supports a mix of sources rather than a single one.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Discusses how the timing and variability of supply and demand justify a mix of sources, with sustained reasoning linked to all three sources.

sampleAnswers.answer: Demand is highest in the evening, but solar power stops at dusk, so the solar farm alone cannot meet demand. Wind power also varies, so a mix of sources is needed to cover gaps in supply.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Discusses the need for more than one source with some links to the scenario, so it meets the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Demand is highest in the evening, and the town has a solar farm.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies a pattern of demand and a source of supply with limited link, so it meets the 2-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Describe the major water reservoirs located within the atmosphere, geosphere, hydrosphere and biosphere

prompts.question: Using the scenario, CLASSIFY each of the four water stores as being in the atmosphere, geosphere, hydrosphere or biosphere.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A Year 11 class walks through a forest after rain and records four stores of water: water vapour rising above the tree canopy, groundwater held in fractured rock beneath the forest, a creek flowing across the forest floor, and water held inside the leaves and roots of the eucalyptus trees.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Classifies all four stores correctly, with a reason from the scenario for each
3 marks: Classifies three stores correctly, with a reason for each
2 marks: Classifies two stores correctly
1 mark: Classifies one store correctly
markerNotes: Classify each store by where the water is held, and name the reservoir, rather than by whether the water is fresh or salty.
Give a short reason for each classification, such as the rock beneath the forest for the geosphere.
commonStudentErrors: Placing the water in the leaves and roots in the atmosphere because it is above the ground.
Naming a reservoir without giving any reason for the classification.

sampleAnswers.answer: The water vapour above the canopy is in the atmosphere, because water vapour is a gas held in the air above the forest. The groundwater in fractured rock is in the geosphere, because it is stored in the solid rock beneath the surface. The creek is in the hydrosphere, because it is liquid surface water that flows across the forest floor. The water inside the leaves and roots is in the biosphere, because it is held within living organisms. Each store is grouped by where the water is held and in what form, not by whether it is fresh or salty, so the classification depends on location.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Classifies all four stores correctly with a reason for each drawn from the scenario, so it meets the top row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The water vapour is in the atmosphere, and the creek is in the hydrosphere.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Classifies two stores correctly without reasons, so it meets the 2-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The groundwater is in the geosphere.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Classifies one store correctly, so it meets the 1-mark row.

prompts.question: Using the scenario, DISTINGUISH between the water reservoirs that hold most of Earth's water and those that hold only a small share.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A class lists the major water reservoirs in a short report: the oceans, which cover most of the planet; the ice caps and glaciers; the groundwater in aquifers; the lakes and rivers; the atmosphere; and the water held by living organisms in the biosphere.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Distinguishes clearly between the large and small reservoirs, with sustained reasoning about their location, salinity and role in the water cycle
5 marks: Distinguishes between the reservoirs with accurate detail and relevant links to the scenario
4 marks: Distinguishes between reservoirs with some relevant detail
3 marks: Describes one large and one small reservoir, each with a relevant feature
2 marks: Identifies a reservoir of large or small volume
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Contrast the reservoirs on a clear basis, such as volume or salinity, rather than listing them one by one.
Explain why the difference matters, such as how quickly water moves through a small store compared with the oceans.
commonStudentErrors: Listing the reservoirs without saying which hold most water and which hold little.
Stating that the atmosphere holds the most water because it is the largest layer of the Earth.

sampleAnswers.answer: The oceans are the largest water reservoir: they hold most of Earth's water, and because the water is salty, it is unavailable for most drinking and irrigation. Ice caps and glaciers hold a large share of Earth's freshwater, but they are a small share of all water and are frozen in place. Groundwater in aquifers is also a major store of fresh water beneath the land surface, although it is much smaller than the oceans. By comparison, the lakes and rivers, the atmosphere and the biosphere each hold only a small share of the total. Water in the atmosphere moves quickly through the cycle, and the water held by living organisms is a tiny share that is continually taken in and released. Distinguishing the water reservoirs by size and by how quickly water moves through them shows that the oceans store water for long periods, whereas the smaller stores are replenished quickly.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Distinguishes the large and small reservoirs on size, salinity and movement through the cycle, with sustained reasoning linked to the scenario.

sampleAnswers.answer: The oceans hold most of Earth's water and are salty. Ice caps hold a large share of freshwater, but they are a small share of all water. The lakes, rivers and atmosphere each hold only a small share.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Distinguishes between reservoirs with some relevant detail, so it meets the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The oceans hold most water, and the atmosphere holds very little.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies a reservoir of large volume and one of small volume, so it meets the 2-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Construct representations to demonstrate how water moves between the major water reservoirs within the atmosphere, geosphere, hydrosphere and biosphere due to water cycle processes

prompts.question: Using the scenario, DEMONSTRATE how rain that falls on the forest moves into the groundwater, by naming each process in order.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: After a storm, a student observes rain falling on a forest. Some water runs off the slope into a creek, some soaks into the soil and moves down to an aquifer, and some is taken up by tree roots and released from the leaves into the air.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Demonstrates the movement of rain into groundwater by naming infiltration, percolation and the transfer to groundwater in order, with links to the scenario
2 marks: Names two relevant water cycle processes linked to the scenario, with limited order
1 mark: Identifies one relevant water cycle process
markerNotes: Name the processes in the order the water moves, so the answer shows the path from the surface to the aquifer.
Name the process, not just the reservoir, such as infiltration for rain soaking into the soil.
commonStudentErrors: Naming evaporation as the process that moves rain into groundwater.
Describing the water cycle in general terms without linking the processes to the storm on the forest.

sampleAnswers.answer: Rain first infiltrates the soil, soaking in through the surface. The water then moves by percolation downward through soil and rock until it reaches the aquifer, which is the groundwater in the geosphere. Water that does not soak in becomes runoff into the creek, while tree roots take up water that is later released by transpiration from the leaves.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Demonstrates the path into groundwater by naming infiltration and percolation in order, with the other processes linked to the scenario.
