dotPoints.description: Evaluate the effectiveness of earthquake detection technologies and warning systems

prompts.question: DESCRIBE how an earthquake detection system uses seismometers and warning systems to alert people in time to act.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A school is learning how an early warning system could alert students before strong shaking arrives at the school.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes how earthquake detection with seismometers detects the first P waves and how warning systems send alerts with a short warning time, with relevant detail
2 marks: Describes one part of an earthquake detection or warning system, without linking the two
1 mark: Identifies seismometers or an early warning system
markerNotes: Describe the signal the system uses, then the alert, then the action it allows.
State that the warning time is short, so the response must be practised.
commonStudentErrors: Stating that early warning systems predict the exact time of an earthquake.
Naming seismometers without saying what they detect.

sampleAnswers.answer: Earthquake detection technologies such as seismometers record the first P waves, which travel faster than the damaging S and surface waves. Warning systems then send alerts before the damaging waves arrive, giving a short warning time of seconds to tens of seconds. This allows people to take protective action, such as dropping and covering.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes seismometers detecting the first P waves, and the warning systems that send alerts with a short warning time.

sampleAnswers.answer: Seismometers detect earthquakes, and a warning is sent to people.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes one part of the system, without explaining the P waves or the warning time.

sampleAnswers.answer: Seismometers are used at volcanoes and in earthquake zones.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies seismometers, but does not describe an earthquake detection or warning system.

prompts.question: ASSESS the effectiveness of earthquake detection and warning systems for a region where most people live far from the epicentre of a likely earthquake.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A city council is deciding whether to fund an earthquake early warning system for a region where most of the population lives far from the main fault.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Assesses the effectiveness of earthquake detection and warning systems for distant populations, weighing warning time, reliability and public response, with a sound judgement
5 marks: Assesses the effectiveness of detection and warning systems, with relevant detail on warning time and reliability
4 marks: Analyses how warning time depends on distance from the epicentre, with some reference to reliability or response
3 marks: Describes a detection or warning feature and its effect on people, with some link to warning time
2 marks: Identifies a detection technology or warning system, without assessing its effectiveness
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about earthquake warnings
markerNotes: Assess by weighing the warning time against the distance from the epicentre, since the value of a warning depends on it.
Note reliability, such as false alarms, and whether people know how to act on a warning.
commonStudentErrors: Stating that warning systems give several minutes of warning to everyone.
Claiming warning systems can predict earthquakes before the first waves are detected.

sampleAnswers.answer: Earthquake detection technologies are effective at finding the location and size of an earthquake quickly, because a network of seismometers can detect the first P waves within seconds. Warning systems use this information to send alerts before damaging waves arrive. Their effectiveness depends on the distance from the epicentre: close to the epicentre the warning time may be only a few seconds, so there is little time to act, while people further away gain more time. Warning systems can also make errors, such as false alarms or underestimating magnitude, which can reduce public trust. Effectiveness further depends on how alerts reach people, whether they know what to do, and whether automatic systems are linked to infrastructure. The council should therefore treat the system as a valuable addition, especially for people far from the epicentre, but not as a replacement for sound building design.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Assesses how warning time, distance from the epicentre, reliability and public response determine effectiveness, and reaches a judgement for distant populations.

sampleAnswers.answer: Warning systems give people some time to act before the shaking arrives. Seismometers detect the earthquake quickly.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes a detection feature and its effect on people, with a link to warning time, but does not assess effectiveness for distant populations.

sampleAnswers.answer: Earthquakes can be detected.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Provides some relevant information about earthquake warnings, with no assessment of effectiveness.

dotPoints.description: Explain how prediction technologies and warning systems are used to minimise the impacts of tsunamis

prompts.question: OUTLINE two prediction technologies used to detect a tsunami and the role of a warning system in reducing its impacts.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A coastal town in a Pacific island nation lies about 900 km from a deep ocean trench. Its warning centre receives earthquake data within minutes of a large undersea earthquake, and deep-ocean pressure sensors then record a wave moving towards the coast.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Outlines two prediction technologies and how each detects or confirms a tsunami, and links the warning system to reducing impacts on the community
3 marks: Outlines two prediction technologies with a relevant link to the warning system
2 marks: Identifies one prediction technology or a warning system and its role in a tsunami
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Name each technology and say what it detects, such as earthquake size and location from seismometers or the pressure change of a wave from deep-ocean sensors.
Link the detection to the warning system, because a confirmed forecast is what allows alerts and evacuation before the impacts arrive.
commonStudentErrors: Describing sirens and evacuation routes without naming any technology that detects a tsunami.
Saying an earthquake by itself proves a tsunami will hit, without explaining that wave or sea-level data must confirm it.

sampleAnswers.answer: Two prediction technologies work together. Seismometers detect the earthquake within minutes and estimate its location and magnitude, which shows whether it could generate a tsunami. Deep-ocean pressure sensors then record the pressure change as a wave passes overhead and send the data by satellite, which confirms the tsunami and forecasts its arrival time. The warning system turns these forecasts into alerts, such as sirens and phone messages, so residents can evacuate to high ground before the impacts reach the coast.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row by outlining two technologies and how each detects or confirms the tsunami, then linking the warning system to reducing impacts on the community.

sampleAnswers.answer: Seismometers detect earthquakes, which can show that a tsunami may form. The warning system then alerts people on the coast.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying one technology and the warning role. It names no second technology and does not explain how the wave is confirmed.

sampleAnswers.answer: Sirens tell people to move to high ground when a tsunami is coming.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by providing some relevant information about tsunami warnings. It names no prediction technology, so it does not outline how a tsunami is detected.

prompts.question: ASSESS how effectively prediction technologies and warning systems reduce the impacts of a tsunami on this council's coast, and identify one limitation the council should address.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A council on a low-lying coast is reviewing its tsunami plan. Its detection relies on seismometers and deep-ocean pressure sensors, but its only tide gauge is 40 km from the main beach. Some residents do not receive phone alerts.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Assesses how well the detection and warning systems reduce tsunami impacts, using the scenario, and identifies a specific limitation with a justified action for the council
5 marks: Assesses the effectiveness of the technologies and warning systems with relevant reference to the scenario
4 marks: Explains how the technologies and warning systems reduce impacts, with some judgement of their limits
3 marks: Describes the technologies or warning systems with some link to reducing impacts
2 marks: Identifies a technology or warning feature relevant to a tsunami
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Judge the systems against the scenario: the early earthquake data is strong, but the distance of the tide gauge and the gaps in phone alerts weaken the warning.
A limitation earns marks only when it is tied to the impacts on people, such as residents who cannot be warned in time to evacuate.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the detection technologies without judging how well they reduce impacts.
Listing limitations the scenario does not give, instead of using the tide gauge distance or the residents without phone alerts.

sampleAnswers.answer: The detection system is effective for the earthquake and the first warning. Seismometers locate and size an earthquake within minutes, so the warning system can start alerting people before a tsunami arrives. Deep-ocean pressure sensors then confirm the wave in open water, so the council can issue, upgrade or cancel alerts with more certainty. These prediction technologies therefore reduce impacts when they work as designed. The main limitation is the tide gauge: it records sea level at a different site, so it cannot give accurate arrival times for the main beach. Residents without phone alerts also miss the warning. Tsunami waves can reach nearby beaches within minutes of an earthquake, so every minute of delay in the alert matters, and each gap in the system leaves people with less time to evacuate. The council should add a closer tide gauge, sirens and door-knock plans, so the warning system reaches every person who needs to evacuate.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by assessing how well the detection and warning systems reduce impacts, and identifies the distant tide gauge as a specific limitation with a justified action. The answer uses the scenario throughout.

sampleAnswers.answer: Seismometers and deep-ocean pressure sensors give the warning system early information about a tsunami, so alerts can be issued quickly. However, the tide gauge is far from the beach, so arrival times for the main beach are less certain.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining how the technologies reduce impacts and giving some judgement of the tide gauge's limits. It does not weigh the gaps in phone alerts or propose an action.

sampleAnswers.answer: Seismometers detect earthquakes, which helps the warning system. Phone alerts also tell people to leave.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying a technology and a warning feature relevant to a tsunami. It does not explain how either reduces impacts.

dotPoints.description: Explain the causes and physical impacts of tropical cyclones, east coast lows, bushfires, droughts, floods and hailstorms in Australia

prompts.question: OUTLINE the cause and one physical impact of an east coast low that affects the New South Wales coast.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A Year 12 student is writing about severe weather on the NSW coast. Her notes say an east coast low can form over the ocean near the coast, bringing strong winds and heavy rain to coastal towns.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Outlines the cause and one physical impact of an east coast low, distinguishing it from a tropical cyclone
2 marks: Identifies the cause or one physical impact of an east coast low
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: An east coast low is non-tropical and forms off the coast, so it does not need the warm tropical water that a cyclone needs.
Give a physical process as the impact, such as flooding or coastal erosion, rather than a social effect.
commonStudentErrors: Describing a tropical cyclone's cause and impacts as if they apply to an east coast low.
Naming heavy rain as the cause, without explaining the low pressure system that produces it.

sampleAnswers.answer: An east coast low is a non-tropical low pressure system that forms over the ocean near the coast, unlike a tropical cyclone, which needs warm tropical water. Its cause is a deepening low that creates a strong pressure gradient and drives strong winds onshore. Its main physical impact is heavy rain that causes flooding, along with coastal erosion from large waves.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by outlining the cause and one physical impact, and distinguishes the low from a tropical cyclone. It is brief and accurate.

sampleAnswers.answer: An east coast low forms near the coast and brings strong winds. Heavy rain can cause flooding.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying a cause and one physical impact. It does not outline how the low develops.

sampleAnswers.answer: East coast lows bring bad weather to the NSW coast.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by providing some relevant information. It names no cause or physical impact.

prompts.question: DISTINGUISH between the causes and physical impacts of a tropical cyclone and a hailstorm that affect the same town.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A regional town on the Queensland coast is hit by a tropical cyclone in January and, several months later, by a hailstorm from a severe thunderstorm in spring. Residents want to understand how the two events differ in cause and physical impact.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Distinguishes the causes and physical impacts of the two events, explaining how their mechanisms and scale differ
5 marks: Distinguishes the causes and physical impacts of both events with relevant reference to the scenario
4 marks: Explains a difference in cause or physical impact between the two events
3 marks: Describes the causes or physical impacts of both events with some comparison
2 marks: Identifies one cause or physical impact of a tropical cyclone or a hailstorm
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Compare the mechanisms: the cyclone needs warm ocean water and rotation, while the hailstorm needs updrafts inside a thunderstorm.
Show how the difference in scale changes the impacts, such as a whole coastline and several days of flooding against brief local damage.
commonStudentErrors: Treating the hailstorm as a small tropical cyclone with the same warm-water cause.
Listing the causes and impacts of each event without comparing them.

sampleAnswers.answer: The two events differ in cause. A tropical cyclone forms over warm ocean water, usually above about 26 degrees Celsius, where rising humid air releases heat and the Coriolis effect starts it rotating. A hailstorm forms within a strong thunderstorm, where updrafts carry water droplets high into freezing air and layers of ice build up before the stones fall. An east coast low, by contrast, is non-tropical and forms over the ocean near the coast, so the cyclone's warm-water cause does not apply to it. Their physical impacts also differ in scale and type. The cyclone brings very strong winds, a storm surge that floods low coastal land, and heavy rain that causes river flooding over several days. The hailstorm is local and brief, but its stones can damage roofs, vehicles and crops within minutes. The cyclone threatens the whole town and its coast, while the hailstorm damages particular property and crops.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by distinguishing the causes and physical impacts of the two events and explaining how their mechanisms and scale differ. The answer also separates the east coast low from both events.

sampleAnswers.answer: A tropical cyclone forms over warm water, while a hailstorm forms in a thunderstorm. The cyclone causes flooding from heavy rain, but the hailstorm damages roofs and crops.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining a difference in cause and a difference in physical impact. It does not explain the mechanisms or the difference in scale.

sampleAnswers.answer: A cyclone forms over warm water. Hail damages roofs and crops.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying one cause and one physical impact. It does not compare the two events.

dotPoints.description: Assess the effectiveness of current forecast modelling and warning technologies for predicting the impact of, and preparing for, tropical cyclones and east coast lows

prompts.question: Explain how ONE technology used to monitor meteorological activity can be used to predict short-term extreme weather events.
markerNotes: Name the technology, say what it measures, then link that measurement to a forecast of a short-term event such as heavy rain or a storm.
Choose an event with a short timescale, such as flash flooding or a severe storm, rather than a long-term hazard such as drought.
commonStudentErrors: Describing a technology without linking it to any prediction.
Naming drought or climate change, which are long-term, instead of a short-term extreme event.
Explaining the physics of the technology in detail when the question asks how it predicts an event.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Explains how a technology can be used to predict a short-term extreme weather event
2 marks: Describes a technology used in weather prediction OR Outlines a technology used in weather prediction AND identifies a short-term extreme weather event
1 mark: Outlines a technology used in weather prediction OR a short-term extreme weather event

sampleAnswers.answer: Doppler Radar can determine how far away a rain cloud is, how fast it is moving and how much rain is falling. If the rainfall is especially heavy, a prediction of areas at risk of flooding over the next few hours can be produced.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining how Doppler radar's measure of rain and movement can predict flooding over the next few hours.

sampleAnswers.answer: Doppler radar sends out microwave pulses and detects those reflected by raindrops in storms. It is used in weather forecasting to show rainfall.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by describing a technology used in weather prediction: “Doppler radar sends out microwave pulses”. It does not explain how its data predicts a short-term extreme event, such as flooding from heavy rain, which the 3-mark row needs. Explaining how the rain and storm movement it measures can predict flooding would lift it to the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Weather satellites take images of clouds.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by outlining a technology used in weather prediction. It names no short-term extreme event and no prediction.

dotPoints.description: Analyse meteorological factors affecting the frequency and severity of floods, droughts and bushfires

prompts.question: DESCRIBE two meteorological factors that increase the severity of a bushfire on a hot day.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student compares two days in a dry eucalypt forest. On the first day the temperature is mild, humidity is high and the breeze is light. On the second day the temperature is high, humidity is very low and strong winds blow.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes two meteorological factors, temperature and humidity, and explains how each increases bushfire severity or frequency
2 marks: Identifies one meteorological factor and its effect on a bushfire
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Name the factor and say how it changes the fire, such as dried fuels igniting more easily, rather than just naming the weather.
Keep to two factors if the question asks for two; a third factor adds words but no marks.
commonStudentErrors: Naming a factor such as wind without saying how it changes the bushfire.
Describing the drought or flood effects when the question asks about a bushfire on a hot day.

sampleAnswers.answer: Two meteorological factors matter most. High temperature dries the fuels, such as leaf litter and grass, so they ignite more easily and bushfires spread faster. Low humidity removes moisture from the fuels and the air, which increases the severity of the fire once it starts. Hot, dry conditions also raise the frequency of ignitions that can grow into a bushfire.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing two meteorological factors, temperature and humidity, and explaining how each increases bushfire severity or frequency. The answer is short and accurate.

sampleAnswers.answer: High temperature dries fuels so fires ignite more easily. Low humidity makes the bushfire more severe.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying one factor and its effect on a bushfire. It gives the second factor only briefly, without explaining its effect on frequency.

sampleAnswers.answer: Hot weather can start a bushfire.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by providing some relevant information. It names no meteorological factor.

prompts.question: DISCUSS how El Niño and La Niña affect the frequency and severity of droughts and floods in eastern Australia, and the bushfire risk that follows drought.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A regional council in eastern Australia is preparing its seasonal risk plan. Climate outlooks suggest a developing El Niño for the coming spring, and the council's records show floods after several years of La Niña conditions.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Discusses how El Niño and La Niña shape the meteorological factors behind drought, flood and bushfire risk, with judgement about how far the phases explain variation between seasons
5 marks: Discusses the effect of El Niño and La Niña on drought or flood frequency and severity, with relevant reference to the scenario
4 marks: Explains how El Niño or La Niña changes rainfall or temperature in eastern Australia
3 marks: Describes an effect of El Niño or La Niña on drought or flood, with some link to the scenario
2 marks: Identifies El Niño or La Niña as a driver of rainfall in eastern Australia
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Name each phase, state its effect on the trade winds or rainfall, and link it to drought or flood rather than only describing the climate event.
Use the scenario: the forecast El Niño and the flood record during La Niña give the judgement something specific to test.
commonStudentErrors: Stating that El Niño causes drought in every season, without considering the timing of the phase or the variation between events.
Confusing the phases, such as saying La Niña brings drought to eastern Australia.

sampleAnswers.answer: El Niño and La Niña are phases of the El Niño-Southern Oscillation, and they change the meteorological factors behind drought and flood in eastern Australia. During El Niño the trade winds weaken and warm water shifts east across the Pacific, so the rain-bearing systems move away from the continent. Eastern Australia usually receives less rain, particularly in spring, which raises the frequency of drought. Drought also dries soils and fuels, and higher temperatures increase the severity of any bushfire that starts. During La Niña the trade winds strengthen and carry more moisture across the continent, so rainfall is usually above average. Saturated catchments then respond strongly to heavy rain, which increases the frequency and severity of floods. Each phase shifts the risk, though its effect on any single season varies.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by discussing how each phase shapes the meteorological factors behind drought, flood and bushfire risk. It judges that the phases shift the risk without fixing it for every season.

sampleAnswers.answer: During El Niño, the trade winds weaken and less rain falls over eastern Australia, which raises the frequency of drought. During La Niña, extra rain saturates the catchments and increases the chance of floods.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining how each phase changes rainfall in eastern Australia. It does not discuss the bushfire link or judge how far the phases explain variation.

sampleAnswers.answer: El Niño brings drier conditions and La Niña brings wetter ones.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying the two phases as drivers of rainfall. It does not explain the effect on drought or flood.

dotPoints.description: Explain how anthropogenic climate change, improper fire management, water overuse and changing land use impact the frequency and severity of floods, droughts and bushfires

prompts.question: OUTLINE how each of the four human influences in the scenario changes the frequency or severity of floods, droughts or bushfires.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A regional council lists four human influences on its hazard risk: anthropogenic climate change, improper fire management, water overuse and changing land use. It wants a brief summary for residents of how each one affects floods, droughts and bushfires.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Outlines how all four human influences change the frequency or severity of floods, droughts or bushfires, with a specific mechanism for each
3 marks: Outlines three of the human influences, each with a specific effect on a hazard
2 marks: Identifies two human influences and a general effect on floods, droughts or bushfires
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Give one mechanism for each influence, such as more runoff from paved land, rather than saying only that it is harmful.
Say which hazard each influence changes, because the question asks about floods, droughts or bushfires.
commonStudentErrors: Listing the four influences without explaining how any of them changes a hazard.
Describing the causes of climate change in general instead of its effect on the hazards.

sampleAnswers.answer: Anthropogenic climate change raises temperatures and alters rainfall patterns, which increases the frequency of droughts and the severity of bushfires. Improper fire management, such as skipping hazard reduction burning, lets fuel load build up, so bushfires burn more intensely when they start. Water overuse lowers river flows and groundwater, which makes droughts more severe and reduces the water available for fighting fires. Changing land use, such as clearing vegetation and paving over floodplains, speeds runoff, so heavy rain produces floods more often and with greater severity.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row by outlining all four influences, each with a specific mechanism for the hazard it changes. The answer is concise and uses the scenario's terms.

sampleAnswers.answer: Climate change makes droughts more frequent. Changing land use speeds runoff, which makes floods more severe.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying two influences and their effects on floods and droughts. It does not address fire management or water overuse.

sampleAnswers.answer: Water overuse affects rivers and groundwater.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by providing some relevant information. It gives no effect on floods, droughts or bushfires.

prompts.question: ASSESS the relative contribution of anthropogenic climate change and improper fire management to the frequency and severity of bushfires in the scenario's region.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A state fire agency has cut hazard reduction burning in a national park for ten years. Over the same decade, its climate report shows hotter, drier summers and more days of extreme fire weather.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Assesses the relative contribution of climate change and fire management to bushfire frequency and severity, with a supported judgement on which is broader and which the agency can control
5 marks: Assesses both influences with relevant reference to the scenario and some judgement of their relative effect
4 marks: Explains how climate change or fire management affects bushfire frequency or severity, with a link to the scenario
3 marks: Describes both influences with some link to bushfire risk
2 marks: Identifies one influence that affects bushfire frequency or severity
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: A judgement must be supported: say which influence is broader, then say which one the agency can change, and why.
Use the scenario's details, such as ten years of reduced burning and more days of extreme fire weather, to test each influence.
commonStudentErrors: Treating climate change and fire management as equal influences without judging which is broader.
Assessing only the causes of bushfires, without considering how fuel build-up changes their severity.

sampleAnswers.answer: Anthropogenic climate change and improper fire management both influence bushfire risk, but they act on different parts of the fire. Climate change raises temperatures and lengthens dry periods, which increases the frequency of days with extreme fire weather and the potential severity of any fire that starts. Improper fire management, here the cut in hazard reduction burning, lets fuel load build up with dead leaves and bark, so fires that start burn hotter and spread further. Judged on the scenario, climate change is probably the broader influence, because it shifts conditions across the whole region in every season. However, the fuel load is the factor the agency controls, so restoring burning would lower severity even as the climate warms. Water overuse and changing land use also matter for floods and droughts, but the scenario gives no direct evidence of their effect on bushfire frequency.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by assessing the two influences on bushfire frequency and severity and making a supported judgement about which is broader and which the agency can control. It is limited to the evidence in the scenario.

sampleAnswers.answer: Hotter, drier summers from climate change raise the frequency of extreme fire weather. Cutting hazard reduction burning lets fuel build up, so fires that start are more severe.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining how each influence affects bushfire frequency or severity, linked to the scenario. It does not weigh one influence against the other.

sampleAnswers.answer: Climate change makes summers hotter and drier.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying one influence that affects bushfire risk. It gives no effect on frequency or severity.

dotPoints.description: Analyse the impact of Cultural burning on the reduction of bushfire disasters

prompts.question: Outline TWO ways in which Cultural burning reduces the fuel load available to a bushfire.
prompts.scenario: Cultural burning is a traditional land management practice used by First Nations peoples in Australia for thousands of years. It involves lighting small, cool fires at particular times of year to manage the landscape.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Outlines TWO distinct ways Cultural burning reduces fuel load and so limits bushfire disasters
2 marks: Outlines one way Cultural burning reduces fuel load OR Identifies two relevant effects of Cultural burning
1 mark: Identifies Cultural burning as a fire management practice
markerNotes: Give a mechanism for each way: removing dead fuel from the ground, or creating a patchwork of burnt areas that breaks up continuous fuel.
Stay with fuel load and fire spread. The question asks how the burning reduces fuel available to a bushfire.
commonStudentErrors: Describing Cultural burning as a general fire-fighting method rather than a deliberate, low-intensity practice.
Stating that Cultural burning removes all fire from the landscape, which misdescribes its purpose.
Giving two ways that are really the same mechanism, such as removing leaves and removing grass.

sampleAnswers.answer: Cultural burning removes dead grass, leaves and litter from the forest floor, which lowers the fuel load available to a later bushfire. Burning in small, patchy mosaics across the landscape also creates breaks in the fuel, so a fire has less continuous fuel to spread through. Both effects reduce the risk of bushfire disasters.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by outlining two distinct ways the practice reduces fuel load, and linking them to the limit on bushfire disasters.

sampleAnswers.answer: Cultural burning removes dead grass and leaves, which lowers the fuel load.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by outlining one way Cultural burning reduces fuel load. It does not give a second distinct way, which the 3-mark row needs.

sampleAnswers.answer: Cultural burning is a traditional fire practice.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying Cultural burning as a fire management practice. It does not say how the practice reduces fuel.

prompts.question: Assess the extent to which Cultural burning can reduce the impact of bushfire disasters during extreme weather.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A national park has used Cultural burning across part of its area for several years. During an extended heatwave with strong winds, a fast-moving bushfire crosses both the burnt and the unburnt sections of the park.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Assesses the extent to which Cultural burning reduces bushfire disasters, weighing its benefits against its limits in extreme weather and reaching a supported judgement
5 marks: Assesses the benefits and limits of Cultural burning for reducing bushfire impact, with specific reference to the scenario
4 marks: Explains how Cultural burning reduces bushfire impact, with some reference to its limits
3 marks: Describes a benefit of Cultural burning for reducing bushfire impact
2 marks: Identifies a way Cultural burning relates to bushfires
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Weigh benefits against limits: fuel reduction and breaks help, but they cannot stop a fire in extreme weather.
Use the scenario as evidence for your judgement, for example that the fire crossed both burnt and unburnt sections.
commonStudentErrors: Writing only about benefits and never assessing the limits of Cultural burning.
Claiming Cultural burning prevents all bushfires, which overstates the evidence.
Ignoring the extreme weather in the scenario when judging the outcome.

sampleAnswers.answer: Cultural burning reduces bushfire disasters where it is applied widely and repeated regularly. Low-intensity burns remove the dead grass and litter that feed fires, and mosaic burning creates a patchwork of areas burnt at different times, which slows spread. The scenario shows that the fire crossed both burnt and unburnt areas, so treated land did not stop it. In extreme weather, such as an extended heatwave with strong winds, fuel is very dry and embers can travel across breaks, so even treated areas can burn. The benefit therefore depends on the extent, timing and frequency of burning, and on the weather at the time. Cultural burning reduces the severity of bushfires but cannot prevent large fires in extreme weather, so it works best alongside other fire management.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by weighing the benefits of mosaic and low-intensity burning against their limits in extreme weather, and reaching a supported judgement. The scenario is used as evidence.

sampleAnswers.answer: Cultural burning removes dead fuel from the ground, which can reduce the impact of a bushfire.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by describing a benefit of Cultural burning. Explaining how removing fuel slows the fire, and noting a limit in extreme weather, would lift it to the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Cultural burning is a practice used in some areas.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by providing some relevant information. It does not link the practice to bushfires or to their impact.

dotPoints.description: Conduct a secondary-source investigation to analyse the effectiveness of technologies used to predict and manage the impact of floods, droughts and bushfires

prompts.question: Outline TWO features of a secondary source you would check before using it to investigate the effectiveness of a flood warning system.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student is investigating whether a new flood warning system reduced property damage in a river town. They have found a government report, a news article and a conference paper that each describe the system.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Outlines TWO distinct features of a secondary source and links each to how reliable the evidence on effectiveness is
2 marks: Outlines one relevant feature of a secondary source OR Identifies two features without relating them to effectiveness
1 mark: Identifies a feature of a secondary source
markerNotes: Name a feature, such as the author's expertise or the methods used, then say what it tells you about whether an effectiveness claim can be trusted.
Choose features that can be checked in a written source, rather than features of the flood warning system itself.
commonStudentErrors: Listing features, such as a title or page count, that do not affect the reliability of the evidence.
Assessing the flood warning system itself rather than the secondary source that describes it.
Naming a primary source, such as the student's own field measurements, when the question asks about secondary sources.

sampleAnswers.answer: A secondary source should name its author, who should have relevant expertise, such as a government agency or a peer-reviewed researcher. This makes its claims about effectiveness more credible. The methodology should also be clearly explained, showing how the effectiveness of the flood warning system was measured and what data were used, so the evidence can be checked.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by outlining two distinct features, the author and the methodology, and linking each to how far the evidence on effectiveness can be trusted.

sampleAnswers.answer: The author should have relevant expertise on flood warnings.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by outlining one relevant feature of a secondary source. It does not check the methods, which would give a second feature and reach the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Check the publication date.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying a feature of a secondary source. It does not say why the feature matters for effectiveness.

prompts.question: Assess the validity of the conclusion that the flood warning system reduced flood damage, using the secondary source described.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A secondary source reports that a new flood warning system reduced flood damage in one river town. It does not report how many warnings were issued, how many residents left early, or how damage was measured before the system was installed.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Assesses the validity of the conclusion by identifying gaps in the evidence, such as missing warning data and no before-and-after comparison, and reaches a supported judgement
5 marks: Assesses the conclusion with reference to at least two limitations of the secondary source
4 marks: Explains one limitation of the secondary source and how it affects the conclusion
3 marks: Describes a feature of the secondary source and its relevance to effectiveness
2 marks: Identifies a feature of the secondary source
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Test the conclusion against the evidence given: what is missing, and what would be needed to show the system caused the reduction.
A judgement of validity should be qualified, for example partly valid, and supported by specific gaps in the source.
commonStudentErrors: Accepting the conclusion because the source is published, without testing the evidence.
Calling the source biased without showing how the missing details affect its conclusion.
Assessing whether flood warnings are useful in general rather than the validity of this conclusion.

sampleAnswers.answer: The validity of the conclusion is limited. The secondary source reports reduced flood damage in one town, but it gives no direct evidence that the flood warning system caused the change. It does not state how many warnings were issued or how many residents left early, so there is no way to tell whether the warnings were acted on. Damage is also not described as measured before the system was installed, so there is no baseline for comparison. Without a comparison town or an earlier period, other factors, such as a smaller flood or better building standards, could explain the lower damage. One case study also cannot show the effectiveness of the system elsewhere. The source is therefore weak support, and an independent comparison is needed before the claim can be accepted.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by identifying specific gaps in the evidence, including missing warning data and no baseline, and reaching a qualified, supported judgement of validity.

sampleAnswers.answer: The secondary source describes lower flood damage after the flood warning system was installed. This is relevant to effectiveness, but it does not say how damage was measured.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing a feature of the source, its claim about damage, and its relevance to effectiveness. Explaining how the missing measurement details limit the conclusion would lift it to the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The source is about flood warnings.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by providing some relevant information about the source. It does not assess the conclusion.

dotPoints.description: Explain how heat energy is stored and distributed by ocean currents and ocean circulation

prompts.question: DESCRIBE how the East Australian Current moves heat energy from the tropics towards southern Australia, and how ocean circulation completes the transfer.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student is studying the ocean off the east coast of Australia. She notes that a strong current flows southward from the Coral Sea, carrying warm water away from the tropics, and that the deep ocean is much colder.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Describes how the East Australian Current and wider ocean circulation store and move heat energy from the tropics, with the link to climate
3 marks: Describes how ocean currents move heat energy from one region to another
2 marks: Identifies ocean currents or ocean circulation as a means of moving heat energy
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Name the current and its direction, and say where the heat comes from and where it goes.
Include the return flow: a full answer explains that the transfer is a circulation, not a one-way movement.
commonStudentErrors: Describing ocean currents as moving cold water to the tropics, reversing the direction of the East Australian Current.
Saying the ocean stores heat without explaining the role of currents or the ocean's high heat capacity.

sampleAnswers.answer: The East Australian Current carries warm water southward from the Coral Sea, transferring heat energy from the tropics towards cooler southern waters. The upper ocean stores much of this heat energy, because the ocean holds far more heat than the atmosphere, and ocean currents move it from place to place. Ocean circulation completes the transfer: cold, dense water sinks in polar regions and flows back towards the equator at depth. In this way ocean currents and ocean circulation redistribute heat that would otherwise build up in the tropics.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row by describing the current's route, how the upper ocean stores heat energy, and the return flow of ocean circulation. It links the transfer to climate.

sampleAnswers.answer: Ocean currents move warm water away from the tropics.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying ocean currents as a means of moving heat. It does not describe the East Australian Current or the return flow.

sampleAnswers.answer: Warm water flows along the coast.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by providing some relevant information. It does not explain how heat energy is moved.

prompts.question: ANALYSE how a slowdown in ocean circulation would change the storage and distribution of heat energy and the climate of coastal regions.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A marine scientist's model shows that a major ocean circulation pattern could weaken over the coming decades. Coastal communities in the study region rely on mild winters and steady rainfall.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses how a weaker circulation changes heat storage and transport, and links these changes to specific effects on coastal climate
5 marks: Analyses the effect of a weaker circulation on heat distribution with relevant reference to the scenario
4 marks: Explains how ocean currents move heat energy and how a change would affect coastal regions
3 marks: Describes the effect of a change in ocean circulation on heat energy with some link to climate
2 marks: Identifies ocean circulation as a store or carrier of heat energy
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Separate the two effects: less heat moving poleward warms the tropical ocean, while regions fed by warm currents cool.
Link each effect to the scenario's communities, such as colder winters or shifted rainfall, rather than describing the ocean alone.
commonStudentErrors: Describing ocean circulation without saying how a slowdown changes heat storage or transport.
Predicting that a weaker circulation warms every coast, which ignores the regions that depend on warm currents.

sampleAnswers.answer: A slowdown in ocean circulation would reduce the poleward transport of heat energy, so less heat would leave the tropics for higher latitudes. The ocean would store more heat energy near the equator, where warm surface water would remain and the upper layers would warm further. Regions that normally receive warm water would cool, because ocean currents such as the East Australian Current carry heat from warmer to cooler waters. Coastal communities would feel this through their seasons: mild winters could become colder and rainfall patterns could shift, because ocean temperature influences the moisture that reaches the land. The ocean's capacity to store heat energy means these effects build slowly, so the climate would change over decades rather than in a single season. The model therefore suggests that a weaker circulation would reshape coastal climate, and this should be tested against observed ocean data.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by analysing the change in heat storage and transport and linking it to specific coastal effects. The answer separates the warming of the tropics from the cooling of regions fed by warm currents.

sampleAnswers.answer: A weaker circulation would move less heat energy from the tropics, so the upper ocean would warm near the equator. Coastal areas that receive warm currents would cool, and their winters would become colder.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining how the change moves heat energy and how coastal regions would be affected. It does not weigh the effects on rainfall or the time over which they build.

sampleAnswers.answer: Ocean circulation carries heat energy from the tropics towards the poles.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying ocean circulation as a carrier of heat energy. It does not explain the effect of a slowdown.

dotPoints.description: Relate changes in ocean currents to the effects of El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) on the Australian climate and the timescales in which these effects occur

prompts.question: OUTLINE how El Niño changes ocean currents across the Pacific and the rainfall of eastern Australia, and the timescales on which ENSO events recur.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A Year 12 student is preparing a timeline of El Niño events for a school project on Australian drought. She has records of ocean temperature, trade wind strength and rainfall in eastern Australia.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Outlines how El Niño changes ocean currents and eastern Australian rainfall, and the irregular timescales of ENSO events
2 marks: Identifies a change in ocean currents or rainfall linked to El Niño
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Name the link in the chain: trade winds, then warm water, then rainfall, rather than listing El Niño effects separately.
Give the timescale as a range of years, and note that each event usually lasts about a year.
commonStudentErrors: Stating that El Niño occurs every year, rather than irregularly.
Describing La Niña's effects when the question asks about El Niño.

sampleAnswers.answer: During El Niño the trade winds weaken, so the warm surface water and ocean currents that normally sit near northern Australia shift east across the Pacific. Rain-bearing storms follow the warm water, so the Australian climate in the east becomes drier, particularly in spring. The timescales are irregular: ENSO events recur roughly every two to seven years and usually last about a year.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by outlining the change in ocean currents, the effect on eastern Australian rainfall and the irregular timescales. It is brief and accurate.

sampleAnswers.answer: El Niño weakens the trade winds and moves warm water east. This reduces rainfall in eastern Australia.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying a change in ocean currents and its rainfall effect. It does not give the timescale.

sampleAnswers.answer: El Niño brings drier conditions to Australia.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by providing some relevant information. It names no change in ocean currents.

prompts.question: ASSESS how changes in ocean currents during ENSO events affect the Australian climate, and how far the timescales of these changes can be predicted.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A regional water authority in eastern Australia is planning for dry years. Its planning relies on ENSO models, but its records show that the timing and strength of El Niño events vary from one event to the next.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Assesses how changes in ocean currents during ENSO drive shifts in the Australian climate, with a supported judgement on how predictable the timescales are
5 marks: Assesses the link between ENSO-related current changes and Australian rainfall or temperature with relevant reference to the scenario
4 marks: Explains how ENSO changes ocean currents and affects the Australian climate
3 marks: Describes an ENSO-related change in ocean currents with some link to the Australian climate
2 marks: Identifies El Niño or La Niña as an ENSO event that affects Australian rainfall
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Make a judgement about predictability: the phases recur irregularly, so the timing of the next event is uncertain.
Tie each current change to a climate effect in eastern Australia, rather than describing the Pacific alone.
commonStudentErrors: Treating El Niño as a fixed cycle that can be forecast precisely for any season.
Assessing the Pacific currents without linking them to rainfall or temperature in Australia.

sampleAnswers.answer: Changes in ocean currents are the link between ENSO and the Australian climate. During El Niño the trade winds weaken, the equatorial ocean currents slow, and the warm water pool shifts east across the Pacific. This moves the rain-bearing systems away from the continent, so eastern Australia usually becomes drier. La Niña reverses the pattern: stronger trade winds push warm water west, and more rain falls over the country. The timescales of these changes are irregular, with events recurring every few years and typically lasting about a year, so the timing of the next El Niño is hard to predict far ahead. The water authority's ENSO models are useful for seasonal planning, but they carry uncertainty about the strength and timing of each event, so dry-year planning should allow for variation rather than assume a fixed outcome.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by assessing how ocean current changes shape the Australian climate and judging how predictable the timescales are. The answer uses the scenario's models to support the judgement.

sampleAnswers.answer: El Niño weakens the trade winds and moves warm water east, so ocean currents change and eastern Australia becomes drier. Its timescales are irregular, so the next event cannot be forecast precisely.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining how ENSO changes ocean currents and affects the Australian climate. It does not assess the scenario's models or weigh their strength.

sampleAnswers.answer: El Niño brings drier conditions to eastern Australia.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying El Niño as an ENSO event that affects Australian rainfall. It gives no current change.

dotPoints.description: Describe the role of Atlantic meridional overturning circulation (AMOC) and thermohaline circulation in the regulation of global climate and the timescales in which these effects occur

prompts.question: Use Graph 1 to outline the conditions in the North Atlantic Ocean under the present climate.
markerNotes: Read Graph 1 at the label "Present climate" and state two conditions, such as salinity and freshwater input, in the words the graph supports.
Describe the level of each condition, such as high or moderate, from the graph's position, without giving a numerical value the graph does not show.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the curve as a whole instead of the position of the present climate.
Using Graph 2 for the condition of the ocean, when Graph 2 shows the strength of the current.
Giving a numerical value for salinity or density that the graph does not provide.

2 marks: Identifies TWO present conditions in the North Atlantic Ocean
1 mark: Identifies ONE condition

sampleAnswers.answer: Relatively high density with a moderate amount of fresh water input.

sampleAnswers.answer: The water has a high density.

The North Atlantic Deep Water (NADW) overturning current forms in the North Atlantic Ocean as warm salty water cools and sinks. It is one of the main drivers of the Great Ocean Conveyor Belt and influences the climate of Europe.

prompts.question: Variations to the NADW overturning current can change climate in Europe. Explain a likely flow-on effect of this change.
