Trees draw water from the soil by transpiration, which draws heat from surrounding air to evaporate water from the tree’s leaves. This cools the air around the tree, reducing local warmer temperatures. Mines produce large quantities of tailings, waste material which can escape causing dust pollution in the air and contaminating waterways. Tailings are stored in dams. During mine reclamation the tailings dam is covered in topsoil and trees are planted over the dam. Tree roots stabilise the soil, which contains the tailings by preventing erosion. Choosing native trees also provides habitat. Planting deep rooted native trees is very effective in combating climate change because they capture CO2, act as a carbon sink and lower local temperatures. Trees successfully contain mine tailings protecting the surrounding environment.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 8-mark row by explaining how native trees address two unrelated problems, climate change through carbon capture and mine tailings through root stabilisation, and by making a supported judgement.

sampleAnswers.answer: Planting native trees is effective against climate change. Trees take in CO₂ during photosynthesis and store carbon in their wood, which reduces the CO₂ in the atmosphere. Transpiration also draws heat from the surrounding air, which cools the local area. However, trees take many years to store a large amount of carbon, so planting is a slow response to rising temperatures.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4–5 row by showing sound knowledge of how planting trees solves one problem, and by making a judgement. Only one problem is used, so the answer does not reach the 6–7 row; a second unrelated problem with a supported judgement would lift it.

sampleAnswers.answer: Native trees are good for the environment because they take in carbon dioxide and provide habitat for animals.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2–3 row by showing basic knowledge of the benefits of trees. No environmental problem is named and no judgement is made, so it does not reach the 4–5 row.

prompts.hscSection: Section II (80 marks). Attempt Questions 21–35. Allow about 2 hours and 25 minutes for this section.

dotPoints.description: Use examples to assess the role of international cooperation and agreements in reducing greenhouse emissions

prompts.question: OUTLINE the aim of the Paris Agreement and one way that countries contribute to it.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student is preparing a short summary of the Paris Agreement for her class. She notes that it asks each country to set its own emission targets and to report on its progress.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Outlines the Paris Agreement's aim of limiting warming and describes one way countries contribute through their own emission targets
2 marks: Identifies the aim of the Paris Agreement, or one way that countries contribute to it
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: State the aim in terms of the temperature goal, such as holding warming well below 2 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels.
Name one contribution, such as each country setting its own emission targets and reporting progress.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the Paris Agreement as a binding treaty that sets the same targets for every country.
Stating the aim without naming any way countries contribute.

sampleAnswers.answer: The aim of the Paris Agreement is to hold the increase in global average temperature well below 2 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels, and to pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5 degrees, which requires lower greenhouse emissions. Countries contribute through international cooperation by setting their own emission targets and reporting on their progress, which the agreement makes transparent.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by outlining the temperature aim and one way countries contribute through their emission targets.

sampleAnswers.answer: The Paris Agreement aims to limit global warming, and countries set their own targets.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying the aim and one contribution. It gives no temperature goal.

sampleAnswers.answer: The Paris Agreement is an international agreement about climate change.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by providing some relevant information. It names no aim or contribution.

prompts.question: ASSESS the role of the Kyoto Protocol and the Paris Agreement in reducing greenhouse emissions, using the examples in the scenario.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student is preparing a report on how two international agreements have affected greenhouse emissions. One agreement set legally binding targets for some developed countries, and the other asks every country to set its own emission targets and report on progress.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Assesses the role of the Kyoto Protocol and the Paris Agreement in reducing greenhouse emissions, weighing binding and national targets and their participation, using the scenario examples
5 marks: Assesses the role of both agreements in reducing emissions, with reference to their targets or participation
4 marks: Explains how one agreement sets targets that influence emissions, with some reference to the other
3 marks: Describes the targets set by the Kyoto Protocol or the Paris Agreement
2 marks: Identifies the Kyoto Protocol or the Paris Agreement as an international agreement on emissions
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Contrast the agreements by how targets are set, binding for Kyoto and national for Paris, and by who takes part.
Assess effectiveness with examples from the scenario, such as the limited participation in Kyoto, rather than saying agreements either work or fail.
commonStudentErrors: Saying the Kyoto Protocol and the Paris Agreement have the same binding targets for all countries.
Describing each agreement without assessing its role in reducing greenhouse emissions.

sampleAnswers.answer: The Kyoto Protocol and the Paris Agreement show two approaches to international cooperation on greenhouse emissions. The Kyoto Protocol set legally binding emission targets for developed countries, which created a clear obligation to reduce emissions over its commitment periods. Its role was significant because it established the principle of binding targets, but its reach was limited: several major emitters did not take on targets, and one party later withdrew. The Paris Agreement asks every country to set its own emission targets and report on progress, so it includes all parties. Its strength is this broad participation and a goal of holding warming well below 2 degrees Celsius. However, because each country sets its own targets, the reduction in greenhouse emissions depends on whether countries strengthen their ambition over time. Overall, the Kyoto Protocol gave binding commitments to a smaller group, while the Paris Agreement provides wider participation with weaker enforcement, so both are needed for effective international cooperation.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by assessing both agreements' targets and participation, using the scenario examples to weigh binding against national targets.

sampleAnswers.answer: The Kyoto Protocol set binding emission targets for some developed countries, while the Paris Agreement asks every country to set its own targets. This widens international cooperation, but the targets may be weaker.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining how each agreement sets targets and the effect on cooperation. It does not assess the effect on emissions.

sampleAnswers.answer: The Kyoto Protocol and the Paris Agreement both aim to reduce greenhouse emissions.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying both agreements as emission-reduction agreements. It offers no assessment.

dotPoints.description: Discuss the role of the 4 pillars of sustainability in maintaining society and the environment

prompts.question: OUTLINE the four pillars of sustainability named in the council plan in the scenario.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A regional council's sustainability plan is built on four pillars: environmental, social, economic and governance. The plan states that every waste strategy must be judged against all four before it is adopted.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Outlines each of the four pillars and its contribution to maintaining society and the environment
2 marks: Identifies the four pillars of sustainability without explaining their contribution
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Name all four pillars and say what each one protects, rather than naming only the environment.
Link each pillar to society or the environment, so the answer shows how the pillars maintain both.
commonStudentErrors: Listing three pillars and omitting governance from the answer.
Describing sustainability as only protecting the environment, without the social or economic pillars.

sampleAnswers.answer: The four pillars of sustainability in the plan are environmental, social, economic and governance. The environmental pillar protects ecosystems and the air and water they depend on, while the social pillar supports the wellbeing of society. The economic pillar keeps the waste service affordable, and governance ensures that decisions are transparent and accountable.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by outlining each pillar and its contribution to society and the environment.

sampleAnswers.answer: The plan has environmental, social, economic and governance pillars.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying the four pillars. It does not explain what each contributes.

sampleAnswers.answer: Sustainability has several parts that support society.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by providing some relevant information. It names no pillar.

prompts.question: DISCUSS how the four pillars of sustainability interact to maintain society and the environment in the council's household waste strategy.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: The council's waste strategy proposes a food-scraps collection that produces compost for local farms. It would cost ratepayers more in the first year, reduce landfill use and cut methane emissions, and create local jobs. Some residents worry that the compost could carry contaminants.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Discusses how the four pillars interact in the strategy, weighing a trade-off between pillars and how governance and testing keep the strategy sustainable
5 marks: Discusses how the strategy serves at least two pillars and identifies a trade-off between them
4 marks: Explains how the strategy serves the environmental or social pillar, with some reference to the economic cost
3 marks: Describes how the compost program affects the environment or society
2 marks: Identifies an effect of the waste strategy on society or the environment
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Treat the pillars as interacting: a gain for one pillar can cost another, so judge the strategy as a whole rather than one pillar at a time.
Use the scenario's specific trade-off, such as first-year cost against landfill savings, rather than listing general benefits.
commonStudentErrors: Listing the four pillars without showing how they interact in the strategy.
Judging the strategy only on cost, which ignores the environmental and social pillars.

sampleAnswers.answer: The four pillars of sustainability work together, so a strategy that strengthens one pillar can weaken another. The environmental pillar is served by the compost program because it reduces landfill use and cuts methane emissions from decomposing food, which protects the air and soil. The social pillar is served by local jobs and by a waste service that residents use and trust, which helps maintain society. The economic pillar is a trade-off, because the first-year cost to ratepayers must be weighed against savings from smaller landfill use over time. The governance pillar requires the council to test the compost for contaminants and report the results openly, which answers residents' concerns and keeps the program accountable. The strategy maintains society and the environment only if all four pillars are considered together, because a cheap program that contaminates farmland would fail the environmental and social pillars, even if it saved money.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by discussing how the pillars interact, weighing the first-year cost trade-off and showing how governance and testing keep the strategy sustainable.

sampleAnswers.answer: The compost program helps the environment by reducing landfill and methane, but it costs ratepayers more in the first year, so the economic pillar is a trade-off.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining the environmental benefit and the economic cost. It does not address the social pillar or governance.

sampleAnswers.answer: The compost program supports the environment and local jobs, which helps society.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying effects on the environment and society. It does not discuss any trade-off.

dotPoints.description: Explain how aspects of sustainability are achieved using Australian renewable and non-renewable resources

prompts.question: EXPLAIN how the wind farm and the rehabilitated mine site in the scenario achieve an aspect of sustainability.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A regional town is replacing a coal-fired power station with a wind farm on former farmland. It is also rehabilitating an open-cut mine site nearby, returning the disturbed land to native vegetation.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Explains how using a renewable resource and rehabilitating a mine site achieve an aspect of sustainability, linking each to an environmental or economic benefit
2 marks: Identifies a renewable or non-renewable resource and an aspect of sustainability it achieves
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Explain the mechanism for each: the wind farm replaces fossil fuel generation, while rehabilitation restores land after a non-renewable resource is extracted.
Name the aspect of sustainability each one achieves, such as lower emissions or restored habitat.
commonStudentErrors: Saying a wind farm is sustainable because wind never stops blowing, without linking it to emissions.
Describing mine rehabilitation as making mining renewable.

sampleAnswers.answer: Replacing the coal-fired station with a wind farm is a sustainable use of a renewable resource, because wind is replenished and the electricity produced has far lower carbon dioxide emissions. This achieves the environmental aspect of sustainability and supports energy security for the town. The rehabilitated mine site, once a non-renewable resource has been extracted, returns the land to native vegetation, which restores habitat and reduces the long-term environmental cost of mining.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining how the renewable resource and the rehabilitated mine site each achieve an aspect of sustainability.

sampleAnswers.answer: A wind farm uses a renewable resource and produces little carbon dioxide.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying a renewable resource and its emissions benefit. It does not discuss the mine site.

sampleAnswers.answer: Wind is a renewable energy source.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by providing some relevant information. It names no aspect of sustainability.

prompts.question: ANALYSE the trade-offs between renewable and non-renewable resource use in the scenario, with reference to the sustainability of each.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A regional town is weighing two options. The first is to keep operating its coal mine for another 20 years, which supplies jobs and export income. The second is to expand a wind farm and solar project on the same land, which is renewable but produces less income and needs storage to supply power when the wind is calm.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses the trade-offs between the non-renewable and renewable options, weighing their economic, social and environmental sustainability and how a planned transition balances them
5 marks: Analyses the trade-offs between the two options with reference to their sustainability
4 marks: Explains a benefit and a drawback of one option in terms of sustainability
3 marks: Describes a feature of the coal mine or the wind and solar project in the scenario
2 marks: Identifies the coal mine as non-renewable, or the wind and solar project as renewable
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Set the short-term economic gain of the non-renewable option against the long-term sustainability of the renewable option.
Use the scenario's details, such as the need for storage, to show the limits of each option rather than listing general pros and cons.
commonStudentErrors: Treating coal as sustainable because it provides jobs and income in the short term.
Assuming that a renewable option has no costs, and ignoring storage and lower income.

sampleAnswers.answer: The trade-off is between the short-term economic benefits of a non-renewable resource and the long-term sustainability of renewable options. Keeping the coal mine for another 20 years provides jobs and export income, but coal is a non-renewable resource, so its reserves will eventually be exhausted and its emissions add to climate change. The environmental and social costs of closure must be planned for, because the town depends on the mine's income. The wind farm and solar project are renewable, so their energy supply does not run out and their operation produces little carbon dioxide. However, their output is intermittent and their income is lower, so the town would need storage to supply power when the wind is calm and the sun is down, and storage adds cost and materials. The sustainability of each option therefore depends on how the town manages its transition. A planned shift from the coal mine to renewable energy, with storage and retraining, achieves more of the economic, social and environmental aspects of sustainability than either option alone. The council should weigh these factors, not simply choose the option with the higher short-term income.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by weighing the economic, social and environmental sustainability of both options and how a planned transition balances them.

sampleAnswers.answer: Coal provides jobs and income, but it is non-renewable and adds emissions. A wind farm is renewable, but it needs storage to supply power when the wind is calm.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining a benefit and drawback of each option. It does not weigh the transition as a whole.

sampleAnswers.answer: The coal mine gives jobs, but coal is a non-renewable resource.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying the coal mine as non-renewable. It gives no analysis of the trade-off.

dotPoints.description: Conduct a secondary-source investigation to analyse the factors affecting the sustainability of a water resource, mining resource, forestry product and agricultural product

prompts.question: Assess the effect of TWO human activities on the sustainability of water resources.
markerNotes: Name two human activities and, for each, the effect on the water resource and how that effect limits its future use, which is the sustainability link.
Add a judgement of how sustainable each activity is, with a reason, to move above description.
commonStudentErrors: Describing two activities without saying what they do to the water resource.
Giving the effect on water but not linking it to sustainability or future use.
Discussing water pollution in general without naming a human activity.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Assesses the effect of TWO human activities on water resources; Clearly links these activities to sustainability
4 marks: Assesses the effect of TWO human activities on water resources; Implies a link to sustainability
3 marks: Explains the effect of ONE human activity on a water resource; Implies a link to sustainability; Provides or implies a judgement OR Describes the effect of TWO human activities on water resources; Provides or implies a judgement
2 marks: Outlines an effect humans have on a water resource
1 mark: Provides some relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer: Sustainability involves meeting the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their needs. Pollution is a human activity that adds litter and chemicals to waterways, such as microplastics, agricultural run-off or oils from transport. This negatively impacts the sustainability of water as a resource as it blocks waterways and reduces water quality for aquatic organisms. The reduction in water quality makes the water unsafe for humans to use in the future. Off-creek water storage dams, where water is taken from rivers during high-flow with good quality and stored for future use is a very sustainable practice. This ensures water-flow and quality in rivers during times of drought, whilst meeting the needs of a community for access to water.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row by assessing the effect of two human activities, pollution and off-creek water storage, and clearly linking each to the sustainability of water.

sampleAnswers.answer: Agricultural run-off carries fertilisers and chemicals into rivers. These nutrients can cause algal blooms, and when the algae die and decay they use up oxygen, which harms fish and other aquatic organisms. This reduces water quality for people as well, so the practice is not sustainable in the long term because future users cannot rely on clean water.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining the effect of one human activity on a water resource: “use up oxygen”. It implies a link to sustainability and gives a judgement. A second activity with its own effect and judgement would reach the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Water is an important resource that many people depend on.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by providing some relevant information. It names no human activity and no effect on the water resource, so it does not outline an effect.

prompts.hscSection: Section II (80 marks). Attempt Questions 21–35. Allow about 2 hours and 25 minutes for this section.

dotPoints.description: Examine the sustainability and resilience of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples’ food systems

prompts.question: Describe ONE resource management process used by Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander Peoples.
markerNotes: Name one traditional practice and describe how it is carried out, then show how it keeps the resource available for later use.
Keep to one process. A list of practices with no description stays in the lower rows.
commonStudentErrors: Describing a modern conservation program, such as a national park, rather than a traditional process.
Naming a practice without saying how it manages the resource.
keywords: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes ONE resource management process used by Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander peoples
2 marks: Outlines a traditional resource management process
1 mark: Provides some relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer: Midden building enables the management of food resources such as shellfish. A midden is a collection of refuse, such as shells and bones left as information for the next group to visit the place. The midden indicates what species have been eaten to allow populations to recover.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing a named traditional process, midden building, and how it manages a food resource so that populations can recover.

sampleAnswers.answer: Cultural burning is a traditional way of managing the land and its resources. It is practised across Australia and has been used for many thousands of years.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by outlining a traditional resource management process: “Cultural burning is a traditional way of managing”. It does not describe how the practice is carried out or how it keeps resources available, which the 3-mark row needs. Describing what the fire does to the land and its plants and animals would lift it to the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Aboriginal Peoples have long managed the land.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by providing some relevant information about Aboriginal land management. It names no process, so it does not reach the 2-mark row.

prompts.hscSection: Section II (80 marks). Attempt Questions 21–35. Allow about 2 hours and 25 minutes for this section.

dotPoints.description: Conduct a secondary-source investigation to assess the viability of producing useful materials from household waste

prompts.question: DESCRIBE two useful materials that could be produced from household food and garden waste, using the secondary sources in the scenario.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A council's review of secondary sources summarises three studies. One reports that separated food and garden waste can be composted into soil conditioner. Another reports that food waste can be fed to anaerobic digesters to produce biogas. The third reports that plastic contamination makes the recovered material costly to sort.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes two useful materials, compost and biogas, that can be produced from separated household waste, using the secondary sources
2 marks: Identifies compost or biogas as a useful material produced from household waste
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Name two useful materials and describe how each is made from the separated waste.
Refer to the secondary sources, such as the study on anaerobic digesters, rather than giving general knowledge only.
commonStudentErrors: Describing household waste as useful in itself, without a process that turns it into a product.
Naming a material that is not produced from household waste, such as metal from car bodies.

sampleAnswers.answer: Compost is a useful material made from separated food and garden waste. It can be used as a soil conditioner that improves soil structure and returns nutrients to it. Biogas is another useful material, produced when food waste is broken down by anaerobic digesters, and it can be burnt for energy. The secondary sources therefore show that both are realistic products of household waste when it is separated.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing two useful materials and how each is made from separated household waste, using the secondary sources.

sampleAnswers.answer: Compost is a useful material that can be made from household waste.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying compost as a useful material. It describes neither product nor the sources.

sampleAnswers.answer: Household waste can be used for something.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by providing some relevant information. It names no material.

prompts.question: ASSESS the viability of producing compost and biogas from household waste in the council's program, using the secondary sources in the scenario.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A council is considering a food and garden waste program. Its review of secondary sources reports that separated food waste can produce compost and biogas, but that plastic contamination lowers the value of the compost and adds sorting costs. It also reports that a biogas plant would need a steady supply of food waste to be economical.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Assesses the viability of compost and biogas production using the secondary sources, weighing technical feasibility against contamination, sorting costs and the need for a steady supply
5 marks: Assesses the viability of the program with reference to contamination or supply, using the secondary sources
4 marks: Explains one product and a factor that affects its viability, with some reference to the sources
3 marks: Describes compost or biogas as a product of separated household waste
2 marks: Identifies compost or biogas as a product that can be made from household waste
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Judge viability on both technical feasibility and economic factors, such as contamination and sorting costs, using the secondary sources in the scenario.
Name the specific limit on each product, such as the need for a clean and steady supply for biogas, rather than saying the program might not work.
commonStudentErrors: Assuming that because compost and biogas can be made, the program is viable.
Ignoring contamination, even though the secondary sources report it as the main economic risk.

sampleAnswers.answer: The viability of producing compost and biogas from household waste depends on the quality and steady supply of the separated material. The secondary sources show that compost and biogas are technically achievable products of household waste, so the technical case is sound. However, contamination is the main economic risk. Plastic in the food and garden waste lowers the value of the compost and adds sorting costs, which can outweigh the revenue from selling the product, so the council would need a clean collection stream or effective sorting to keep the program viable. The biogas plant is more sensitive to supply: it requires a steady volume of food waste to operate economically, and seasonal changes or low participation would reduce its output. The viability is strongest where the council can secure clean, separated waste and a market for both products. The secondary sources support a pilot program with monitoring of contamination and output before the council commits to a full plant, because the evidence on costs and yields is limited.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by weighing technical feasibility against contamination, sorting costs and supply, and using the secondary sources to support the judgement.

sampleAnswers.answer: Compost and biogas can be produced from separated household waste, but plastic contamination adds sorting costs, so the program is viable only with clean waste.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining the products and one factor affecting viability. It does not weigh supply or give a judgement on the pilot.

sampleAnswers.answer: Compost and biogas are both products that can come from household waste.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying the products. It gives no judgement of viability.

dotPoints.description: Use examples to explain how a circular economy can contribute to sustainable consumption and production

prompts.question: EXPLAIN what a circular economy is and how it differs from a linear economy, using the example in the scenario.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A furniture company stops selling new tables only. It collects old tables, repairs and resells them, and recycles the timber from any that cannot be repaired.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Explains the circular economy and contrasts it with a linear economy, with an example from the scenario
2 marks: Identifies reuse, repair or recycling as features of a circular economy, or describes a linear economy
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Define the circular economy by its features, such as reuse, repair, remanufacture and recycling, and contrast it with the take-make-dispose pattern.
Use the furniture example to show a product kept in use, rather than only defining the terms.
commonStudentErrors: Defining a circular economy as simply recycling, without reuse or repair.
Describing a linear economy as one that does not produce waste.

sampleAnswers.answer: A circular economy keeps products and materials in use for as long as possible, through reuse, repair, remanufacture and recycling, so waste is designed out of the system. A linear economy takes resources, makes products and disposes of them. In the scenario, the furniture company repairs and resells old tables and recycles timber that cannot be repaired, which is an example of a circular economy. This supports sustainable consumption and production because fewer new resources are extracted.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining the circular economy, contrasting it with a linear economy, and using the furniture example.

sampleAnswers.answer: A circular economy reuses and recycles materials, while a linear economy throws them away.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying reuse and recycling and describing the linear pattern. It has no scenario example.

sampleAnswers.answer: A circular economy is a type of economy that cares about waste.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by providing some relevant information. It gives no features of the circular economy.

prompts.question: ANALYSE how the circular economy approach in the scenario could contribute to sustainable consumption and production, with reference to its effect on waste.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A city's packaging program requires retailers to accept returned glass bottles and clean them for reuse. It also offers repair services for electrical appliances, and a textile collector sends worn clothing that cannot be sold to a fibre recycler. The council is measuring how much waste each program diverts from landfill.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses how the reuse, repair and recycling programs keep materials in use, tracing their effect on new production and on waste, and notes what the benefit depends on
5 marks: Analyses how at least two of the programs contribute to sustainable consumption and production
4 marks: Explains how one program keeps materials in use and reduces new production or waste
3 marks: Describes a program in the scenario and its effect on waste
2 marks: Identifies a reuse, repair or recycling program in the scenario
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Link each program to the stage it affects: reuse displaces new production, repair extends product life, and recycling returns material to production.
Note what the benefit depends on, such as consumers returning bottles, rather than assuming the programs always work.
commonStudentErrors: Describing recycling as the whole of the circular economy, without reuse or repair.
Saying the circular economy eliminates all waste, rather than reducing and keeping materials in use.

sampleAnswers.answer: The circular economy contributes to sustainable consumption and production by keeping materials in use and reducing the extraction of new resources. The bottle return program enables reuse of glass for many cycles, so each returned bottle displaces the production of a new container and reduces the energy and raw materials used in manufacturing. The appliance repair service extends the life of products, which lowers consumption of new appliances and the waste sent to landfill. Clothing that cannot be resold goes to a fibre recycler, so its material re-enters production instead of becoming waste, which reduces the demand for new fibres. Together these programs reduce waste at several stages: fewer products are discarded and materials stay in circulation. The council's measurement of waste diverted from landfill gives evidence of the effect. However, the benefit depends on consumers returning bottles and using repair services, so the programs are most effective when they change buying habits as well as the disposal of waste.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by tracing how each program keeps materials in use and affects new production and waste, and noting what the benefit depends on.

sampleAnswers.answer: Returning glass bottles for reuse and repairing appliances keep materials in use, so fewer new products must be made and less waste goes to landfill.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining how two programs keep materials in use. It does not trace the effect in depth or note what the benefit depends on.

sampleAnswers.answer: Reusing bottles and repairing appliances reduces waste.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying two programs from the scenario. It gives no explanation of their effect.

dotPoints.description: Conduct a secondary-source investigation to evaluate traditional landfill practices and bioreactors as waste management strategies

prompts.question: DESCRIBE how a bioreactor landfill differs from a traditional landfill in the way it manages the breakdown of waste.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A secondary-source review compares two landfill designs. A traditional landfill compacts household waste into cells lined with clay and a plastic liner, with leachate collected and the methane often captured or flared. A bioreactor landfill adds moisture and recirculates leachate to speed the breakdown of organic waste, and it captures the methane for energy.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes how a bioreactor landfill speeds waste breakdown through moisture and leachate recirculation, in contrast with the slower breakdown of a traditional landfill
2 marks: Identifies a feature of a bioreactor landfill or a traditional landfill in managing breakdown
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Describe the mechanism: moisture and recirculated leachate speed decomposition in a bioreactor, while compaction and sealed cells keep it slow in a traditional landfill.
Compare the two designs on the same point, such as the speed of breakdown or the capture of methane.
commonStudentErrors: Stating that a bioreactor landfill stops waste from breaking down.
Describing only the liner of each landfill without explaining how breakdown differs.

sampleAnswers.answer: A bioreactor landfill speeds the breakdown of organic waste by adding moisture and recirculating leachate, which keeps the waste in conditions that favour decomposition. A traditional landfill relies on compaction and a sealed cell, so breakdown is slow and the waste remains in the ground for decades. The methane produced by a bioreactor can be captured and used for energy, which turns the breakdown into a resource.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing how moisture and leachate recirculation speed breakdown in a bioreactor, compared with a traditional landfill.

sampleAnswers.answer: A bioreactor landfill adds moisture to speed up the breakdown of waste.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying a feature of the bioreactor. It does not contrast it with a traditional landfill.

sampleAnswers.answer: Landfill is a place where waste is buried.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by providing some relevant information. It describes no difference in breakdown.

prompts.question: DISCUSS the strengths and limitations of traditional landfill and bioreactor landfill as waste management strategies, using the secondary sources in the scenario.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A secondary-source investigation reports that a traditional landfill has lower operating costs but can release leachate into groundwater if its liner fails. It also reports that a bioreactor landfill produces methane for energy faster, but needs more monitoring and careful control of moisture to avoid odour and leachate problems.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Discusses the strengths and limitations of both landfill strategies, weighing cost, groundwater risk and energy recovery, and reaches a justified conclusion from the secondary sources
5 marks: Discusses a strength and a limitation of both landfill strategies using the secondary sources
4 marks: Explains a strength or a limitation of one landfill strategy, with some comparison to the other
3 marks: Describes a feature of traditional landfill or a bioreactor from the secondary sources
2 marks: Identifies a strength or limitation of one landfill strategy
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Weigh both strategies on the same criteria, such as cost, groundwater risk and energy recovery, so the comparison is clear.
Reach a conclusion that depends on conditions, such as whether energy recovery is valued, and justify it with the secondary sources.
commonStudentErrors: Listing features of each landfill without saying which strengths or limitations matter most.
Calling bioreactor landfills risk-free because they produce energy.

sampleAnswers.answer: Both landfill strategies have strengths and limitations, and the secondary sources show that the choice depends on cost, risk and energy recovery. A traditional landfill has a clear strength in its lower operating costs and simpler management, which makes it practical where budgets are limited. Its main limitation is the risk that leachate escapes into groundwater if the liner fails, and that waste decomposes slowly, so the site must be monitored for decades. A bioreactor landfill has the strength of faster breakdown and the capture of methane for energy, which turns a waste problem into a resource. Its limitations are the need for more monitoring and careful control of moisture, because poorly managed recirculation can cause odour and leachate problems. The bioreactor also has higher operating costs. The secondary sources suggest that the bioreactor is the stronger strategy where energy recovery is valued and the operator can manage it, while the traditional landfill remains a lower-cost option with a higher long-term groundwater risk.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by weighing the strengths and limitations of both strategies on cost, groundwater risk and energy recovery, and reaching a justified conclusion.

sampleAnswers.answer: A traditional landfill is cheaper to run but may leak leachate into groundwater. A bioreactor produces methane for energy but needs more monitoring.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining one strength and limitation of each strategy. It does not reach a conclusion.

sampleAnswers.answer: Traditional landfill is cheaper, but bioreactors can produce methane.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying one strength of each strategy. It gives no limitation or conclusion.

dotPoints.description: Use scientific evidence to justify strategies for the safe management of problem wastes

prompts.question: EXPLAIN why mercury from fluorescent globes must not be placed in general household waste.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A household is clearing out a cupboard and finds old fluorescent globes, a box of used batteries and a tin of old paint. The council's guide says some of these items are problem wastes that need separate handling.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Explains that mercury is toxic and can leach from broken globes into soil or water and accumulate, so it needs safe collection as a problem waste
2 marks: Identifies mercury as toxic, or states that fluorescent globes are a problem waste
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Explain the hazard with scientific evidence: mercury is toxic and can leach and accumulate in food chains.
Link the hazard to the disposal method, such as breakage in landfill releasing mercury into soil or water.
commonStudentErrors: Stating that fluorescent globes are dangerous only because they can break, without naming mercury.
Saying mercury in globes is harmless because the amount is small.

sampleAnswers.answer: Fluorescent globes contain mercury, which is toxic to people and wildlife. When globes go to ordinary landfill, the glass breaks and the mercury can leach into groundwater and soil, where it can accumulate in food chains. The scientific evidence on mercury toxicity is why these globes need collection through a problem wastes program that recovers the mercury safely.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining the toxicity of mercury, its leaching and accumulation, and the need for safe collection.

sampleAnswers.answer: Mercury is toxic, so it should not go into general waste.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying mercury as toxic. It does not explain how it harms the environment.

sampleAnswers.answer: Fluorescent globes are a type of household waste.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by providing some relevant information. It gives no hazard or reason.

prompts.question: JUSTIFY a strategy for the safe management of the problem wastes in the scenario, using scientific evidence about their hazards.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A council runs used-battery, paint and fluorescent globe collections that residents rarely use, and many still put these items in the general bin. The council is deciding whether to add drop-off points at the local supermarket, run a yearly collection day, or require retailers to take back the products. Its summary of hazards covers lithium-ion batteries (fire risk), paint solvents and mercury.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Justifies a strategy for the problem wastes using scientific evidence about each hazard, and explains why the chosen collection method suits how residents behave
5 marks: Justifies a strategy with scientific evidence about at least two hazards
4 marks: Explains a hazard of one problem waste and a strategy that addresses it
3 marks: Describes a hazard of a problem waste in the scenario
2 marks: Identifies a problem waste or hazard in the scenario
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Support each strategy with a specific hazard from the evidence, such as fire risk for lithium-ion batteries or toxicity for mercury.
Justify the collection method against the behaviour it must change, such as the convenience of a drop-off point, rather than saying it is simply safer.
commonStudentErrors: Recommending a strategy without linking it to the hazard it manages.
Saying all problem wastes are dangerous, without specifying why.

sampleAnswers.answer: A product stewardship approach with drop-off points at the supermarket is justified by the scientific evidence on the hazards of these problem wastes, and it supports their safe management. Lithium-ion batteries can short-circuit and catch fire in a bin or a garbage truck, so they must be kept out of general waste and collected in a controlled way. Paint and its solvents contain volatile organic compounds that harm air quality and can contaminate soil and water if disposed of carelessly. Mercury in fluorescent globes is toxic and can leach into groundwater and accumulate in food chains, so the globes need to be recovered intact. A supermarket drop-off point suits these hazards because it is convenient, so residents are more likely to use it than an annual collection day, and the retailer can store the items safely until licensed recyclers collect them. Requiring retailers to take back the products, as some product stewardship schemes do, shifts responsibility to the producer and encourages designs that are safer to recycle. The strategy should combine these measures with public education, because residents need both access and an understanding of the hazards to change their disposal habits.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by justifying the strategy with scientific evidence for each hazard, and explaining why drop-off points suit residents' behaviour.

sampleAnswers.answer: Lithium-ion batteries can catch fire and mercury is toxic, so the council should provide drop-off points for these problem wastes.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining two hazards and a matching strategy. It does not justify the choice against alternatives.

sampleAnswers.answer: Batteries and mercury are hazards, so they should not go in the general bin.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying two hazards from the scenario. It gives no strategy or evidence.

dotPoints.description: Evaluate the effect of waste reduction strategies on the geosphere, atmosphere, biosphere and hydrosphere

prompts.question: DESCRIBE how reducing packaging waste in the scenario affects the atmosphere and the hydrosphere.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A supermarket chain introduces a refill scheme for detergent and cuts its plastic packaging by a third. The remaining packaging is sent for recycling, and the scheme reduces the number of delivery trucks carrying packaging to the store.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes how waste reduction lowers emissions to the atmosphere and reduces plastic entering the hydrosphere, with reference to the scenario
2 marks: Identifies an effect of reducing packaging on the atmosphere or the hydrosphere
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Name the two effects separately: fewer trucks and less manufacturing reduce atmospheric emissions, and less plastic reduces litter in water.
Use the scenario's details, such as fewer delivery trucks, rather than general claims about waste.
commonStudentErrors: Stating that reducing packaging increases emissions because the remaining packaging is recycled.
Describing the hydrosphere only as rainfall, without linking it to plastic in water.

sampleAnswers.answer: Waste reduction through less packaging cuts the emissions from making and transporting packaging, and from fewer delivery trucks, which reduces pollutant gases in the atmosphere. In the hydrosphere, less plastic packaging means less litter and microplastic entering rivers and oceans, so waste reduction protects water quality. The refill scheme therefore reduces the pressure of this waste on both the atmosphere and the hydrosphere.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing the atmospheric and hydrospheric effects of reduced packaging, with reference to the scenario.

sampleAnswers.answer: Less packaging means less plastic in rivers and oceans.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying an effect on the hydrosphere. It does not address the atmosphere.

sampleAnswers.answer: Reducing packaging is good for the environment.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by providing some relevant information. It names no sphere.

prompts.question: EVALUATE how far the waste reduction strategies in the scenario reduce the effects of waste on the geosphere, atmosphere, biosphere and hydrosphere.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A city council introduces three waste reduction strategies: a deposit scheme for drink containers, a ban on single-use plastic bags, and a food waste campaign that cuts the amount of food sent to landfill. A review of the program records lower landfill volumes, fewer plastic bags in waterways and reduced methane emissions from landfill. It also notes that the deposit scheme needs collection trucks, and that some bags have been replaced with thicker plastic bags.
prompts.markingCriteria:
8 marks: Evaluates the effect of the strategies on each sphere, weighing gains against trade-offs such as truck emissions and thicker bags, and reaches a supported overall judgement
7 marks: Evaluates the effects on several spheres with sound reference to the scenario, including at least one trade-off
5-6 marks: Analyses the effect of the waste reduction strategies on at least two spheres with some reference to the scenario
3-4 marks: Describes or explains an effect of a waste reduction strategy on one sphere
2 marks: Identifies an effect of waste reduction on a sphere or a strategy from the scenario
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Evaluate each strategy against each sphere, then weigh the gains and trade-offs, rather than listing effects one sphere at a time.
Use specific scenario evidence for the trade-offs, such as truck emissions and the weight of replacement bags, to support the overall judgement.
Make the judgement follow from the evidence: say which effect is strongest and what would confirm the net benefit.
commonStudentErrors: Listing the effects on each sphere without weighing them against one another.
Assuming every strategy has a net benefit on every sphere, without considering trade-offs.

sampleAnswers.answer: The waste reduction strategies reduce the effects of waste on most spheres, but their overall effect depends on the trade-offs in each. The food waste campaign has the strongest effect on the atmosphere, because less food sent to landfill means less methane from decomposition, which is a potent greenhouse gas. Reduced landfill volumes also lessen the pressure on the geosphere, since less land is needed for burial and there is less leachate risk to soil and rock. The ban on plastic bags protects the hydrosphere, because fewer bags in waterways means less plastic entering rivers and oceans. This benefits the biosphere, since animals that mistake bags for food are less likely to be harmed. The deposit scheme reduces waste by recovering containers, but its collection trucks add diesel emissions to the atmosphere, which partly offsets the gain. The replacement of single-use bags with thicker bags also means more plastic is used per bag, so the benefit to the biosphere and hydrosphere is smaller than the fall in bag numbers suggests. Overall, the strategies reduce the effects of waste on the geosphere, atmosphere, biosphere and hydrosphere, with the strongest gains for methane and plastic litter. The council should measure the net effect, including truck emissions and bag weight, to confirm the overall benefit.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 7-8 mark row by evaluating each strategy against each sphere, weighing trade-offs such as truck emissions and thicker bags, and reaching a supported overall judgement.

sampleAnswers.answer: The food waste campaign reduces methane from landfill, which helps the atmosphere, and the bag ban reduces plastic in waterways, which helps the hydrosphere. The deposit scheme needs trucks, which add emissions, so the net effect is less clear.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by analysing the effect of the strategies on two spheres. It does not evaluate the overall effect.

sampleAnswers.answer: The bag ban reduces plastic in waterways. The food campaign reduces landfill.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying an effect of two strategies. It does not address any sphere in depth.

dotPoints.description: Conduct a secondary-source investigation to identify the essential materials and minerals required to construct photovoltaic cells, wind turbines, electric motors/generators and batteries

prompts.question: DESCRIBE the essential materials needed for wind turbines and for batteries, using the secondary source in the scenario.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A secondary source for a student's investigation lists materials used in renewable energy technologies. It states that wind turbines need steel for towers, copper for generators and rare earth magnets, and that rechargeable batteries commonly use lithium, cobalt, nickel and graphite.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes the essential materials for wind turbines and for batteries, using the secondary source
2 marks: Identifies one essential material for a wind turbine or a battery
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Name at least one material for each technology, using the secondary source in the scenario.
Give the role of each material in the technology, such as copper in the generator, rather than only listing metals.
commonStudentErrors: Naming fossil fuels as the essential materials for wind turbines.
Listing materials without linking them to the technology they build.

sampleAnswers.answer: The secondary source identifies essential materials for each technology. Wind turbines need steel for their towers and copper for their generators, as well as rare earth magnets in some designs. Batteries commonly use lithium, along with cobalt, nickel and graphite, so battery production relies on a small number of minerals.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing the essential materials for a wind turbine and for batteries, drawn from the secondary source.

sampleAnswers.answer: A wind turbine needs steel and copper, and a battery needs lithium.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying materials for both technologies. It gives no role for each material.

sampleAnswers.answer: Wind turbines and batteries need materials from mines.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by providing some relevant information. It names no specific material.

prompts.question: ASSESS the sustainability of relying on lithium and rare earth elements for batteries and electric motors, using the secondary source in the scenario.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student's secondary source reports that demand for lithium and rare earth elements is rising as electric vehicles and wind turbines expand. It notes that mining these minerals uses large amounts of water in some regions, that battery recycling is limited at present, and that a few countries supply most of the world's rare earth elements.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Assesses the sustainability of relying on the minerals by weighing their operating benefits against mining impacts, supply concentration and the limits of recycling
5 marks: Assesses the sustainability of the reliance with reference to mining impacts or recycling
4 marks: Explains one environmental or economic issue with the reliance on lithium or rare earth elements
3 marks: Describes a use of lithium or rare earth elements in batteries or electric motors
2 marks: Identifies lithium or rare earth elements as materials needed for batteries or electric motors
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Weigh the benefits of electric motors and batteries against the impacts of mining, such as water use and land damage, rather than judging only one side.
Use recycling as a test of sustainability: a supply that cannot be recovered from used products depends on continued mining.
commonStudentErrors: Calling electric motors and batteries fully sustainable because they produce no operating emissions.
Listing mining impacts without considering supply concentration or recycling.

sampleAnswers.answer: Relying on lithium and rare earth elements for batteries and electric motors is only partly sustainable. These materials are essential for the transition to renewable energy, and electric motors and batteries have much lower operating emissions than fossil fuel equipment, which is a sustainability gain. However, mining these minerals uses large volumes of water in some regions, and extraction can damage ecosystems and land, which weakens the environmental sustainability of the supply. Lithium and rare earth elements are also concentrated in a few countries, so supply is vulnerable to political and economic disruption, which affects the economic and social sustainability of communities that depend on the industry. Recycling is the key to improving sustainability, because recovering lithium and rare earth elements from used batteries and motors reduces the need for new mining. At present, recycling of batteries is limited, so the sustainability of this reliance depends on investing in recovery and designing products that can be dismantled. The reliance is sustainable only if recycling and responsible mining improve together.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by weighing the operating benefits of batteries and electric motors against mining impacts, supply concentration and the limits of recycling.

sampleAnswers.answer: Lithium and rare earth elements are needed for batteries and electric motors, but mining uses water and recycling is limited, so the supply is not fully sustainable.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining the environmental issue of mining and the limit of recycling. It does not weigh the benefits of the technologies.

sampleAnswers.answer: Batteries and electric motors need lithium and rare earth elements, which come from mining.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying the minerals as needed materials. It does not assess sustainability.

dotPoints.description: Use raw material, land area and mining data to compare the total material use for equivalent nuclear, coal fired, natural gas fired, hydroelectric, solar farm and wind farm electricity generation

prompts.question: Compare the total material use for coal fired electricity generation with that of a solar farm producing the same amount of electricity, referring to raw material, land area and mining.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student compares two power options for a regional town, one coal fired and one solar farm, each supplying the same amount of electricity over a year.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Compares total material use, showing that coal fired generation has higher mining demand from its continuous fuel supply, and that the solar farm uses raw material and land area mainly in construction
2 marks: Compares the raw material or land area of the two methods, with a reference to mining or total material use
1 mark: Identifies that the two methods use different amounts of raw material
markerNotes: Name the source of the raw material for each method, then compare the totals.
Say where the material use occurs: continuous fuel supply for coal, construction for solar.
Give the land area as a comparison, not only a statement that it is large.
commonStudentErrors: Says the solar farm uses no raw material because it runs on sunlight.
Compares only the land area, without the mining demand or the total material use.
Says coal fired generation uses less raw material because the plant is small.

sampleAnswers.answer: Total material use for coal fired generation is dominated by the raw material mined as fuel, which is extracted continuously from mines with a large land area. A solar farm producing the same electricity needs no fuel mining, but its panels and frames contain raw material and it occupies a large land area for its output. Coal fired generation therefore has the higher mining demand, while the solar farm's total material use is mostly in its construction.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row: compares total material use, the continuous mining for coal and the construction materials for solar.

sampleAnswers.answer: A solar farm needs more land area than a coal fired plant, but the coal fired plant needs mining for its fuel.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: compares land area and mining, without a full comparison of total material use.

sampleAnswers.answer: Both methods use some raw material.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row: identifies raw material as used by both methods without comparison.

prompts.question: Analyse the data on raw material, land area and mining for nuclear, coal fired, natural gas fired, hydroelectric, solar farm and wind farm generation, to compare their total material use.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A table gives, for an equal amount of electricity, a qualitative rating of the raw material mined, the land area occupied and the mining disturbance for six generation methods. The nuclear and hydroelectric rows show the least fuel mining, while the solar farm and wind farm rows show the largest land areas per unit of output.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Analyses the data across raw material, land area and mining for all six methods to compare total material use, and notes that each method trades one material demand for another
4 marks: Analyses the data for most of the six methods, comparing total material use with a clear reference to land area and mining
3 marks: Describes the raw material, land area or mining for at least two methods, with limited comparison of total material use
2 marks: Identifies one difference in raw material or land area between the methods
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about generation methods
markerNotes: Analyse all three data types, raw material, land area and mining, before reaching a total.
Name the method with the lowest total material use, and say why.
Conclude that no option avoids material demand, so the trade-off has to be stated.
commonStudentErrors: Says solar farms and wind farms have the lowest total material use because they need no fuel.
Compares only the fuel mining, leaving out land area and construction materials.
Says nuclear generation uses large amounts of uranium per unit of output.

sampleAnswers.answer: Nuclear generation has the lowest total material use for its output, because its fuel is a very small mass of raw material and it occupies a small land area. Its main material demand is the concrete and steel of the plant. Coal fired and natural gas fired generation need continuous mining of fuel, so their total material use over the life of a plant is large, with coal mining also disturbing a large land area. Hydroelectric generation needs a large land area for its reservoir and heavy concrete for the dam, while the solar farm and wind farm need large land areas per unit of output and substantial raw material for panels, towers and turbines. No option is free of mining, so land area and fuel demand must be weighed together when judging total material use.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row: analyses raw material, land area and mining across all six methods and concludes that every option carries a trade-off.

sampleAnswers.answer: Nuclear generation has a small fuel mass and land area, but coal fired generation needs large amounts of fuel mining.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row: describes material demands for two methods, with limited comparison of total material use.

sampleAnswers.answer: Each method uses some raw material.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row: provides relevant information without any analysis.

dotPoints.description: Analyse the demand for fossil fuels in maintaining a non-renewable energy economy, and the impact on mining and carbon dioxide emissions in Australia

prompts.question: Describe how demand for fossil fuels in a non-renewable energy economy affects mining and carbon dioxide emissions in Australia.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A Year 12 student is writing a short paragraph for a class on energy futures, explaining why Australia's fossil fuel demand matters for its mining industry and its emissions.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes how demand for fossil fuels sustains a non-renewable energy economy, how this drives mining in Australia, and how burning the fuels adds carbon dioxide emissions
2 marks: Describes the link between fossil fuel demand and either mining in Australia or carbon dioxide emissions
1 mark: Identifies that fossil fuels are used in Australia's energy supply
markerNotes: Link demand to mining and to emissions in separate sentences.
Name Australia's export role for coal and gas as the reason mining follows demand.
Say that burning the fuel releases carbon dioxide, so emissions follow the same demand.
commonStudentErrors: Says fossil fuels are not mined in Australia, so demand does not affect mining.
Describes carbon dioxide emissions without linking them to fossil fuel demand.
Says renewable energy depends on fossil fuel mining.

sampleAnswers.answer: Demand for fossil fuels sustains a non-renewable energy economy, in which coal and gas supply a large share of the energy used. Australia exports much of its coal and gas, so this demand keeps mining active in Australia. Burning the fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide, so the same demand drives carbon dioxide emissions, and reducing demand would ease both mining and emissions.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row: describes the link between fossil fuel demand, mining and carbon dioxide emissions in Australia.

sampleAnswers.answer: Demand for fossil fuels keeps mining active in Australia, which exports coal and gas.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: describes the link to mining only, without emissions.

sampleAnswers.answer: Fossil fuels release carbon dioxide when they are burned.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row: identifies a property of fossil fuels without linking it to demand or mining.

prompts.question: Analyse how demand for fossil fuels sustains a non-renewable energy economy, and explain one way the link to mining and carbon dioxide emissions in Australia could be weakened.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A state energy plan assumes that coal and gas will continue to supply most electricity for decades, so mining royalties and emissions are projected to stay steady.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Analyses how fossil fuel demand sustains the non-renewable energy economy and its links to mining and carbon dioxide emissions in Australia, and explains a credible way the link could be weakened, including export demand
4 marks: Analyses the links between fossil fuel demand, mining and emissions, with a reasoned way the link could be weakened
3 marks: Explains that fossil fuel demand drives mining and emissions, with limited analysis of how this could change
2 marks: Identifies a link between fossil fuels and mining or emissions
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about energy in Australia
markerNotes: Trace the chain: demand, then mining or burning, then emissions.
Name the way the link could be weakened, and say what effect it would have.
Test the weakening: note whether export demand could still keep mining active.
commonStudentErrors: Says reducing domestic demand always ends mining in Australia.
Says carbon dioxide emissions are unaffected by how much fossil fuel is burned.
Describes the energy plan without analysing the link to demand.

sampleAnswers.answer: Fossil fuels such as coal and gas remain the main energy source in a non-renewable energy economy, because existing power stations, transport fleets and industrial plant depend on them. This demand supports mining in Australia, since a large share of the coal and gas produced is exported to meet demand overseas, and it sustains the carbon dioxide emissions released when the fuels are burned. The link would be weakened if demand for fossil fuels fell, for example through a switch to renewable electricity and electric vehicles, which would reduce the need for fuel mining and cut carbon dioxide emissions. However, export demand from other countries could keep mining active even after domestic demand falls, so the link is not removed by domestic change alone.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row: analyses the chain from demand to mining and emissions, and gives a reasoned weakening that includes export demand.

sampleAnswers.answer: Demand for fossil fuels keeps a non-renewable energy economy running, and burning them releases carbon dioxide.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: explains the drivers of demand and emissions, with no analysis of how the link could change.

sampleAnswers.answer: Australia exports coal and gas.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row: provides relevant information without linking it to the energy economy.

dotPoints.description: Analyse the demand for copper and other critical minerals in the renewable and non-renewable energy economy, and the implications for mining in Australia

prompts.question: Describe the uses of copper and other critical minerals in the renewable and non-renewable energy economy, and their effect on mining in Australia.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A class is asked to explain why copper and other critical minerals are in demand, using a simple example of a solar farm and a coal fired station.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes the uses of copper and critical minerals in both renewable and non-renewable energy systems, and links the demand to mining in Australia
2 marks: Describes a use of copper or a critical mineral in an energy system, with a link to mining
1 mark: Identifies copper or a critical mineral as used in energy systems
markerNotes: Name one use of copper and one use of a critical mineral, and say which economy each supports.
Link demand to mining in Australia in the final sentence.
Name the minerals, not only the category critical minerals.
commonStudentErrors: Says copper is used only in renewable energy.
Says critical minerals are not used in energy systems.
Describes mining without linking it to the demand for minerals.

sampleAnswers.answer: Copper is used in the cabling, motors and transformers of the renewable and non-renewable energy economy alike. Critical minerals such as lithium, cobalt and nickel are used in batteries and some turbine magnets, which support the renewable energy economy, while fossil fuel plants also need copper in their generators and grids. Growing demand for these minerals therefore affects mining in Australia, which produces several of them.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row: describes copper and critical minerals in both kinds of energy system and links demand to mining in Australia.

sampleAnswers.answer: Batteries use critical minerals such as lithium, and demand for lithium affects mining.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: describes one use and links it to mining, without the non-renewable energy economy.

sampleAnswers.answer: Copper is used in electrical cables.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row: identifies a use of copper without linking it to energy systems or mining.

prompts.question: Analyse how the shift from a non-renewable to a renewable energy economy changes the demand for copper and other critical minerals, and the implications for mining in Australia.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A mining company is deciding whether to expand copper and lithium operations in Australia, based on a forecast that the renewable energy economy will grow faster than the non-renewable energy economy.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Analyses how the shift changes demand for copper and critical minerals, showing that some demand falls for fossil fuel infrastructure but rises for renewable technologies, and discusses the implications for mining in Australia
4 marks: Analyses the change in demand for copper or critical minerals across the two economies, with a clear statement of the implications for mining
3 marks: Explains that renewable energy uses copper and critical minerals, with limited reference to the implications for mining
2 marks: Identifies a use of copper or a critical mineral in renewable energy
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about mining
markerNotes: Compare demand across the two economies, not only the renewable one.
Give the implication for mining in Australia as a conclusion, not only a description.
Mention that copper is used in both economies, so total demand is not simply reduced.
commonStudentErrors: Says the shift to renewable energy removes all demand for copper.
Says critical minerals are used in large amounts by fossil fuel power stations.
Describes mining without discussing the implications of the change.

sampleAnswers.answer: A shift from a non-renewable to a renewable energy economy reduces demand for fossil fuel infrastructure, but it increases demand for copper, which is needed in cabling, motors and transmission networks, and for critical minerals such as lithium and nickel in batteries. The renewable and non-renewable energy economy both use copper, so total demand for copper is not simply reduced. Batteries and some wind turbine magnets depend on critical minerals that traditional plants use in much smaller amounts, so demand for these minerals rises as the renewable share grows. For mining in Australia, the implications are growing demand for lithium, copper and nickel, alongside pressure on land, water and approvals, and a need to manage the environmental impacts of expansion.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row: analyses the change in demand across both economies and draws out the implications for mining in Australia.

sampleAnswers.answer: Copper and critical minerals are used in renewable energy, so demand for them rises as the energy mix shifts.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: explains the change in demand, with limited reference to mining in Australia.

sampleAnswers.answer: Copper is used in electrical cables.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row: provides relevant information without analysis of demand or mining.

dotPoints.description: Analyse data to compare the dispatchability, greenhouse gas emissions, wastes and fuel sustainability of operating nuclear, coal fired, natural gas fired, hydroelectric, solar farm and wind farm for electricity generation

prompts.question: Describe the dispatchability, greenhouse gas emissions, wastes and fuel sustainability of operating a coal fired power station and a solar farm for electricity generation.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A council is comparing a coal fired power station with a solar farm for supplying electricity to its region, and needs a short description of each on four measures.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Describes the dispatchability, greenhouse gas emissions, wastes and fuel sustainability of both methods, with a clear contrast between the coal fired station and the solar farm
3 marks: Describes three of the four properties for both methods, with some contrast
2 marks: Describes two of the properties for one or both methods
1 mark: Identifies one property of a method of generation
markerNotes: Take the four properties in order, and contrast the two methods on each.
State that a solar farm is not dispatchable unless storage is added.
Name the waste produced by each method, rather than saying waste in general.
commonStudentErrors: Says the solar farm is dispatchable because it produces power every day.
Says coal fired stations produce no greenhouse gas emissions during operation.
Describes the fuel sustainability of coal without saying whether it is finite.

sampleAnswers.answer: Coal fired generation has high dispatchability, because output can be increased or reduced on demand, whereas a solar farm produces power only when the sun shines unless storage is added. Coal fired operation produces large greenhouse gas emissions, while a solar farm emits almost none during operation. The coal fired plant produces wastes such as fly ash and carbon dioxide, while the solar farm produces little waste in operation but needs disposal of its panels at the end of their life. On fuel sustainability, coal is a finite fossil fuel that must be mined continuously, whereas sunlight is a renewable resource that is not used up.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row: contrasts all four properties for both methods.

sampleAnswers.answer: Coal fired generation produces greenhouse gas emissions, while a solar farm produces few.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: describes two properties, emissions for both methods, with no contrast on the other two.

sampleAnswers.answer: Coal is a fossil fuel.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row: identifies a property of a fuel without describing either method on the four measures.

prompts.question: Analyse the trade-off between dispatchability and greenhouse gas emissions for nuclear, hydroelectric and wind farm generation, and comment on their fuel sustainability.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A council is comparing nuclear, hydroelectric and wind farm options for a regional grid, and wants to know which balances dispatchability with low greenhouse gas emissions.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Analyses the trade-off between dispatchability and greenhouse gas emissions for all three methods, and compares their fuel sustainability, showing which method best balances the two
